title: Expression data from KOPT-K1 cells treated with PPZ or iPAP
summary: T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL) is an aggressive malignancy of early T-cell precursors. We have identified that perphenazine (PPZ), a phenothiazine antipsychotic drug, has anti-tumor potency in T-ALL cells due to its ability to activate the tumor suppressor PP2A. PPZ activates phosphatase activity of PP2A through facilitating the assembly of its three specific subunits, PPP2R1A, PPP2R5E and PPP2CA into one heterotrimeric active PP2A holoenzyme in T-ALL cells. Through biochemical assays, we identified an analogue of PPZ (iPAP: improved PP2A activator, PPZ-derived) that can potently activate PP2A through this mechanism and induce apoptosis in T-ALL cells, but lack the ability to bind and inhibit dopamine receptor D2. This analogue did not induce movement disorders that have limited the usefulness of PPZ as an anti-tumor drug. We used microarrays to detail the global program of gene expression underlying PPZ- and iPAP-mediated cell apoptosis in T-ALL cells.

title: B cell-reactive neoantigens boost immune response in personalized cancer vaccination
summary: The involvement of B cells in neoantigen-driven immunity remains unclear in human cancer. In this work, we characterized >437,000 IgG-binding-tested peptides and >370 million B cell receptor (BCR) clones to develop a method that identifies B cell epitopes. Finally, we constructed a multi-omics model encompassing genomic and transcriptomic features to enhance prediction of clinical benefit of patients receiving immune checkpoint blockade therapy. These results suggest that B cell reactivity is also an important factor in anticancer immunity.

title: ISL1 and AQP5 complement each other to enhance gastric cancer cell stemness by regulating CD44 expression
summary: Gastric cancer, a prevalent and life-threatening malignancy, is believed to involve cancer stem cells as a contributing factor to tumor progression. This study delves into the influence of ISL1 on the stem-like properties of human gastric cancer cells. In human gastric cancer samples, there is an observed elevation in ISL1 expression, which correlates with the expression of stem cell markers, notably LGR5. Functionally, ISL1 fosters the self-renewal, cell proliferation, migration, and the clonogenic potential of gastric cancer cells in vitro. Furthermore, it enhances the ability of these cells to form tumors and metastasize in vivo. Additionally, ISL1 collaborates with AQP5, collectively intensifying the tumorigenicity of gastric cancer cells. Mechanistically, transcriptomic analysis of cells overexpressing ISL1 unveils a notable activation of the FOXO pathway. This activation leads to increased nuclear expression of FOXO3, subsequently resulting in elevated expression of the stemness-associated gene CD44 in gastric cancer cells. These findings shed light on the role of ISL1 in promoting the stem-like characteristics of gastric cancer cells and emphasize the connection between ISL1 and AQP5 as a novel therapeutic target for individuals with gastric cancer.

title: Discovery of a novel inhibitor of macropinocytosis with antiviral activity
summary: Several viruses hijack various forms of endocytosis in order to infect animal cells. Here, we report the discovery of a new molecule with antiviral properties, that we named virolin, which limits viral entry by macropinocitosis. The identification of virolin derives from a chemical screen using High-Throughput Microscopy, where we identified new chemical entities capable of preventing infection with a pseudotype virus expressing the spike (S) protein from SARS-CoV-2. Subsequent experiments confirmed the capacity of virolin to limit infection by actual SARS-CoV-2, as well as by additional viruses, such as Monkeypox or TBEV. Mechanistic analyses revealed that the compound inhibited macropinocytosis, limiting this entry route for the viruses. Importantly, virolin has no significant toxicity to host cells. In summary, we present a new molecule that inhibits viral entry via the endocytic route, offering a new alternative to prevent viral infection.

title: Heme Synthesis Inhibition Induces the Intrinsic Apoptosis Pathway in Leukemia with OSGIN1 Upregulation
summary: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is one of the hematological malignancies with poor outcome. AML owns its unique metabolic status and to find its metabolic vulnerability is warranted. title: BRD3 mediates transcriptional reprogramming in ARID1A-deficient ER+ breast cancer [RNA-seq]
summary: Metastasis is the major cause of breast cancer-related deaths. ARID1A mutations occur in up to 12% of ER+ breast cancer metastasis, resulting in resistance to endocrine therapy, but an unexpected gain in sensitivity to BET inhibitors. Using the mouse intraductal xenografting model we showed that the loss of ARID1A leads to aggressive tumours with elevated metastatic potential and significant changes in chromatin structure and transcriptional profiles. ARID1A-depleted tumours rely less on FOXA1/ER and more on BRD proteins, particularly BRD3. Using a PROTAC targeting BET proteins, we can inhibit ARID1A-depleted tumours and reduce metastatic burden. However, we reveal important limitations with BET inhibitors, as revealed in numerous failed clinical trials. Analysis of other tumour types corroborated the consequences of ARID1A loss observed in breast cancer models, suggesting a pan-cancer ‘over-ride’ mechanism. Collectively, our findings suggest that ARID1A-depleted cancers gain hyper-sensitivity to bromodomain proteins, while also revealing opportunities and limitations with their inhibitors.

title: TRIM24 degradation counteracts adaptation to androgen receptor inhibition in prostate cancer [RNA-seq]
summary: The activation of androgen receptor (AR) signaling is the key lineage-specific oncogenic pathway and the primary therapeutic target in prostate cancer. While the therapeutic responses to androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) and androgen receptor signaling inhibitors (ARSi) are highly variable, disease progression to fatal castration-resistant prostate cancer (CRPC) is, in many cases, inevitable. The latter involves processes such as the reactivation of AR signaling, epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT), and the transformation to AR-negative disease through lineage plasticity. In contrast, little is known about the early adaptation mechanisms in residual disease that initiate these processes, leading to tumor relapse. Here, we identify a critical role for TRIM24 in supporting the survival of residual cancer cell subpopulations primed for tumor relapse in vivo. In agreement, the reduction of TRIM24 through bi-functional degraders (dTRIM24) significantly delays or abrogates the emergence of CRPC related to AR-reactivation and lineage plasticity. Mechanistically, dTRIM24 inhibits AR/mTOR signaling in residual disease but, more importantly, also counteracts adaptive pathways directly engaged by AR inhibition, such as STAT3-signaling and the release of EMT-promoting cytokines. Finally, dTRIM24’s anti-tumor activity also extends to CPRC models with limited therapeutic options. In summary, the findings more broadly position TRIM24 as an effective and druggable target for preventing prostate cancer progression under AR inhibition.

title: U2AF1 S34F enhances tumorigenic potential by exhibiting synergy with KRAS mutation and altering response to environmental perturbations
summary: U2AF1 S34F, a somatic splicing factor mutation, is frequently recurrent in human neoplasias such as lung adenocarcinoma (ADC). Although U2AF1 S34F has been shown to occur early in tumor lineages, the mutation, alone, is insufficient for producing tumors. However, lung ADC patients with U2AF1 S34F frequently have co-occurring KRAS mutations and smoking histories. We hypothesized that U2AF1 S34F interacts with oncogenic KRAS and environmental stress to promote tumor-forming potential. To elucidate interaction of U2AF1 S34F with a co-occurring mutation, we generated human bronchial epithelial cells (HBEC3kts) with U2AF1 S34F or with co-occurring U2AF1 S34F and KRAS G12V. From analyzing short-read transcriptome sequences, we found synergistic effects of co-occurring mutations on gene expression in cell cycle and inflammatory pathways associated with increased tumors in mouse xenografts, anchorage-independent growth, proliferation, and altered cytokine production. Interestingly, HBEC3kts harboring only U2AF1 S34F display increased splicing in stress granule protein genesand increased viability in cigarette smoke concentrate. Our results suggest that U2AF1 S34F may prime cells for transformation by allowing precancerous cells to survive longer when environmental stress is present, permitting U2AF1 S34F cells to accumulate transforming mutations, such as KRAS G12V

title: Collection of CRC cell line grown in vivo
summary: Recent studies revealed the presence of an aggressive subgroup of colorectal cancer (CRC) that exhibits a distinct tumor growth pattern, characterized by high abundance of cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs). To identify cancer cells-intrinsic traits underlie this phenotype and to characterize its stromal features, we generated mouse xenografts from 19 CRC cell lines, where normal mouse stroma cells are recruited and educated by epithelial cancer cells. The in vivo xenograft growth rate showed high variability between cell lines, revealing a subgroup of slow-paced tumors. Cancer cells of this subgroup display distinctive transcriptional features, only partially captured by previously described CRC molecular subtypes, involving epithelial-mesenchymal transition and cooperation with a specific CAF population in remodeling the extracellular matrix. We therefore called the cancer cell signature “epithelial matrix remodeling” (EMR), and the CAF signature “matrix remodeling CAF” (mrCAF). In pan-cancer analysis, the EMR and mrCAF signatures were co-detected and associated with poor prognosis in multiple tumor types. Altogether, these results highlight the intrinsic capability of cancer cells to recruit, educate and cooperate with CAFs, indicating route toward tumor progression involving the interaction between tumor and its microenvironment.

title: Unveiling the role of UPF1-mediated mRNA decay in melanoma tumorigenesis by modulating the miR-101-3p/NANOS1 axis
summary: Numerous studies have reported that Up-frameshift protein 1 (UPF1) as a crucial posttranscriptional regulator in nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD), attributing its role to tumorigenesis across various cancers. However, its recently unveiled function in UPF1-mediated mRNA decay (UMD), intricately coordinated with miRNA, remains unexplored in the context of tumorigenesis. Herein, we elucidate the pivotal role of UPF1 in governing melanoma tumorigenesis by modulation of NANOS1 expression via miR-101-3p. Depletion of UPF1 across three melanoma cell lines significantly impaired cell growth, migration, and invasion by cell cycle arrest and disrupted tumor formation in vivo. Through comprehensive RNA-seq and biochemical analyses, we elucidate that attenuation of UPF1 leads to an increase in NANOS1 expression, consequently suppressing melanoma tumorigenesis. Mechanistically, UPF1 orchestrates the destabilization of NANOS1 via UPF1-mediated mRNA decay (UMD) facilitated by miR-101-3p. Intriguingly, our findings highlight a novel protein modification event involving the phosphorylation of ELK1 by the UPF1/miR-101-3p/NANOS1 pathway, as revealed by antibody microarray analysis. Importantly, our study underscores the significance of UPF1 and NANOS1 in regulating melanoma tumorigenesis, even in drug-resistant cell lines and in vivo models including syngeneic and xenograft mouse models. Collectively, these insights shed light on the role of UMD in melanoma tumorigenesis through the UPF1/NANOS1/miR-101-3p axis and unveil potential therapeutic strategies for both primary and drug-resistant melanoma treatment.

title: Potential of Plasma Cell-Free RNA to Capture Immune Dynamics and Predict GVHD after Hematopoietic Stem Cell Transplantation
summary: Hematopoietic Stem Cell Transplantation (HSCT) is one of the oldest and most successful immunotherapies. Yet, despite long-standing success in the use of HSCT for the treatment of blood cancers and severe immune disorders, monitoring post-transplant complications remains a challenge due to a lack of informative diagnostic tests. Here, we investigate the utility of cell-free RNA (cfRNA) in plasma as a liquid biopsy to monitor allogeneic HSCT recipients during and after treatment. We assayed longitudinal samples from 92 HSCT recipients by cfRNA sequencing and show that cfRNA provides insight into treatment and recovery trajectories, immune dynamics in response to transplantation, infection, and solid-tissue injury associated with Graft-Versus-Host Disease. Collectively, our results provide support for the use of plasma cfRNA profiling to monitor complications of HSCT.

title: Spatial genome and transcriptome co-mapping reveals clonal heterogeneity in tumor tissue [RNA-Seq]
summary: Tumor heterogeneity arises from the sequential acquisition of somatic mutations and the selection of fitter clones, leading to distinct genotypes and phenotypes. summary: DNA methylation is a key epigenetic mark, commonly associated with gene silencing. title: Androgen stimulation rapidly reorganizes 3D chromatin structure and transcription factor binding to trigger AR-mediated gene transcription in prostate cancer [dataset 1]
summary: Background Androgen receptor (AR)-mediated transcription is the primary driver of prostate cancer growth and proliferation. Androgen treatment induces AR binding and recruitment of different AR co-regulator transcription factors, resulting in rapid changes to AR-regulated transcription. However, the temporal epigenetic mechanisms by which AR induces gene expression and the associated chromatin interactions are not completely understood. Results Here, we mapped the fine-scale dynamics of AR binding, 3D chromatin interactions and temporal transcription immediately following treatment with 5α-dihydrotestosterone (DHT) in prostate cancer cells. Our findings show that DHT treatment of hormone-deprived LNCaP cells leads to time-dependent activation of AR binding, differential chromatin interactions, and AR-mediated transcription. Using the MOFA+ statistical framework for integrated multi-omics analysis, we identified three distinct modes of temporal epigenome variation post-DHT treatment: (1) rapid AR binding, (2) transient 3D chromatin interactions, and (3) progressive transcription of androgen-regulated genes. Notably, rapid AR binding sites exhibited increased H3K27ac levels within 5 minutes of DHT treatment, prior to AR/FOXA1 binding. Additionally, we found that highly transient 3D chromatin interactions are pre-marked by CTCF occupancy at enhancers. Furthermore, we demonstrate that nascent gene expression plays a contributory role in the progressive transcription of key canonical AR target genes. Conclusions These findings reveal that androgen stimulation rapidly reorganizes 3D chromatin structure and transcription factor binding to trigger three distinct patterns of temporal epigenome states associated with the establishment of AR-mediated transcription in prostate cancer.

title: Non-canonical RNA binding of the MYBL2 transcription factor promotes melanoma (RNA-seq)
summary: Melanoma originates from melanocytes, and the process of melanocyte malignant transformation is affected by various factors, including non-mutational gene alterations. MYBL2 is a transcription factor primarily known for its role in regulating cell cycle progression. Notably, MYBL2 can also binds RNA, and its oncogenic effect is mediated through its RNA binding function. Crosslinking-immunoprecipitation followed by high-throughput sequencing revealed that MYBL2 primarily binds protein-coding genes and introns. Interestingly, MYBL2 does not affect the RNA metabolism of its direct targets. Instead, its RNA binding function influences its association with chromatin and thereby rewiring the transcription program favoring poor patient survival. Surprisingly, we observed that MYBL2 binds RNA exclusively in melanoma cells, but not in melanocytes. This phenomenon is primarily due to the altered RNA background developed following melanoma transformation, while alternations within MYBL2 itself also involved in a lesser extent. Therefore, our work identified a novel oncogenic function of MYBL2 through its RNA binding activity, extending our current understanding of MYBL2 and highlighting a critical mechanism in melanoma progression.

summary: Biomolecular condensates organize cellular environments and regulate key processes like transcription. title: Colorectal cancer heterogeneity co-evolves with tumor architecture to determine disease outcome
summary: Intratumoral heterogeneity, originating from genetic, epigenetic, and phenotypic cellular diversity, is pervasive in cancer. As these heterogeneous states employ diverse mechanisms to promote tumor progression, metastasis, and therapy resistance, emergence of cancer heterogeneity is one of the most significant barriers to curative treatment. We further combine this approach with spatial transcriptomics, multiplex immunohistochemistry, and patient-derived organoids to uncover a dynamic, co-evolutionary relationship between tumor architecture and cell states. We identify clinically relevant architectural interfaces in CRC tissue that diversify cellular identities by favoring distinct cancer stem cell states and thus promote evolution of tumor heterogeneity. Specifically, tissue fragmentation and associated compressive forces promote loss of classic stem cell (SC) signature and acquisition of fetal/regenerative SC states, which initially emerges as a hybrid state with features of epithelial-to-mesenchyme (EMT) transition. Additional tumor stroma communication then diversifies these states into distinct stem cell and EMT states at the invasive margins of tumors. Reciprocally, Wnt signaling state of tumor cells tunes their responsiveness to tissue architecture. Collectively, our work uncovers a feedback loop between cell states and tissue architecture that drives cancer heterogeneity and cell state diversification. Our machine learning-based analyses harness this co-dependency, independently of mutational status or cancer stage, to predict patient outcome.

title: Comparative in vitro toxicity of nicotine enantiomers and corresponding representative nicotine salts in human lung and nerve cells
summary: Introduction: Synthetic nicotine ((R)-nicotine and (R,S)-nicotine) and corresponding nicotine salts in e-liquids are gradually replacing natural nicotine ((S)-nicotine). However, their toxicological risks remain largely unknown. Aims and Methods: We aim to reveal toxicological profiles of synthetic nicotine and nicotine salts (nicotine benzoate, lactate, and tartrate) based on human lung and neural cells. Results: No significant differences in toxic effects were found among different nicotine or nicotine salt enantiomers. Cytotoxicity of nicotine and nicotine salts to SH-SY5Y cells was higher than that of NCI-H292 cells. Cytotoxicity of nicotine tartrate was the highest, followed by nicotine benzoate and nicotine, and finally nicotine lactate. Risks of DNA and chromosomal damage did not increase. Nicotine primarily induced oxidative stress by depleting glutathione, while nicotine salts generated reactive oxygen species. Varying degrees of mitochondrial hyperpolarization were induced, especially for nicotine benzoate. Nicotine enhanced apoptosis with higher cell membrane permeability, while nicotine salts hardly induced apoptosis. Nicotine induced elevated phosphorylated c-Jun expression, while nicotine salts hardly increased its expression. Kyoto encyclopedia of genes and genomes enrichment analysis of differentially expressed genes showed that nicotine and nicotine salt differentially expressed genes were mainly enriched in growth, division, differentiation, environmental stress regulation response, immune, and antioxidant function pathways, affecting cell growth and development. Conclusions: In vitro toxicological risks of nicotine isomers or salts were similar. Salt forms may enhance or weaken toxicity with different injury mechanisms, involving oxidative stress and apoptosis. Implications: The multidimensional toxicological effects of nicotine enantiomers were similar, but there were significant differences in the toxic effects between nicotine and nicotine salts. Among nicotine salts, the toxicological effects of nicotine benzoate were closest to those of nicotine. Nerve cells were more sensitive to the cytotoxicity, while lung cells appeared to be more sensitive to other cell damage. These findings provide a scientific basis for the industrial application of nicotine enantiomers and nicotine salts.

title: Wee1 opposes APC/CCdh1 activity to promote S-phase entry
summary: Wee1 phosphorylates and inhibits CDK activity and is best understood for its role in inhibiting mitotic entry and the G2 DNA damage checkpoint. Our study reveals a new cell cycle control mechanism and has implications for how Wee1 inhibitors should be used in the clinic.

Cells become secretory, pro-metastatic and alter their cell-to-cell communication behavior. Taken together, these stress response pathways show an adaptive quiescent program and acquired partial EMT, allowing cells to resist loss of ribosome biogenesis, nucleolar architecture and ensure survival and restore homeostasis upon recovery. Correlatively, similar stress adaptions are seen to be contributing to progression of different cancer types especially in breast cancer and AML originating in the later stages of ribosomopathies.

title: circEPSTI1 Enables Dengue Innate Immune Evasion by Sponging miR-942-5p, a Repressor of host AKT1 signaling and the Viral Genome
summary: Circular RNAs (circRNAs) have recently been reported to be crucial regulators of gene expression in several diseases. Their role in dengue remains unexplored. In this study, circEPSTI1 induction was observed in DENV-infected peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) and plasma of dengue patients. circEPSTI1 induction is interferon-dependent, as IRF3-knockout cells completely abolished its induction. circEPSTI1 enhances DENV infection by sponging the expression of hsa-miR-942-5p. The antiviral role of hsa-miR-942-5p is mediated by bidirectional inhibition of conserved genomic sequences of the DENV genome across NS1, NS3, and NS5 and the host AKT1 signaling pathway. Overexpression of the circEPSTI1 relieves the inhibition of has-miR-942-5p over DENV genomic RNA and the host SERPINE1 to activate AKT1 signaling. The activation of AKT1 signaling facilitates DENV survival and enhanced replication. The expression of SERPINE1 and circEPSTI1 was upregulated in Dengue patients, and pharmaceutical inhibition of SERPINE1 through Tiplaxtinin inhibits the DENV replication by reducing the expression of circEPSTI1 and SERPINE1. Overall, therapeutic targeting of circ-EPSTI1-miR-942-5p-SERPINE1-AKT can be beneficial in the dengue treatment.

title: Transcriptomic response to TRIP12 knockdown and HSP90 inhibition in melanoma cells
summary: Melanoma, as a typical cancer, is characterized by high mutational burden and rapid proliferation, both of which contribute to elevated proteotoxic stress and reliance on protein quality control systems. To model this, we used the melanoma cell lines Ma-Mel-102 (differentiated, MLANA- and MITF-expressing, ~1200 missense mutations) and Ma-Mel-94 (dedifferentiated, ~700 missense mutations). This study investigates the role of the E3 ubiquitin ligase TRIP12 in regulating proteostasis in melanoma, particularly under proteotoxic stress induced by inhibition of HSP90, a key molecular chaperone. This dataset provides RNA-seq transcriptomic profiles of Ma-Mel-94 and Ma-Mel-102 cells following siRNA-mediated TRIP12 knockdown, with or without HSP90 inhibition by 17-DMAG.

title: RBM33 Drives AML Leukemogenesis via Leukemogenic Chromatin Remodeling Mediated by eRNA m6A Demethylation [MINT-seq_TT-seq]
summary: Although our previous study showed that RBM33 forms a complex with ALKBH5 and is required for head and neck cancer development, its role in human acute myeloid leukemia (AML) leukemogenesis has remained elusive. Here, we demonstrate that RBM33 is highly expressed in AML and is essential for AML cell survival. RBM33 promotes AML development in an m6A demethylation–dependent manner. Mechanistically, m6A methylation of the eRNAs of the tumor suppressors SEMA3B and SEMA3F facilitates enhancer–promoter interactions through SND1- and PRMT5-mediated histone modifications. High RBM33 expression induces m6A demethylation of SEMA3B and SEMA3F eRNAs, leading to eRNA decay and disruption of enhancer–promoter interactions. Consequently, the expression of SEMA3B and SEMA3F is suppressed, thereby promoting AML cell growth. Collectively, our findings reveal that RBM33 drives AML leukemogenesis by mediating m6A demethylation of tumor suppressor eRNAs, resulting in chromatin state alterations at their loci. This work reveals how RBM33 regulates AML development by coordinating eRNA m⁶A demethylation with histone modification–induced 3D chromatin structural alterations at tumor suppressor loci, highlighting a selective and critical role for RBM33 in AML and opening new avenues for potential therapeutic targeting.

title: Basal marker ΔNp63α is not enriched in pancreatic cancer metastases nor in primary tumors post-chemotherapy
summary: Cancer cells within a single pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) are most often heterogeneous in their expression of the basal or classical transcriptional program. Predominance of the basal subtype has been associated with poorer patient outcomes and increased resistance to chemotherapy. Based on this, we predicted that basal subtype would be enriched in tumors previously treated with chemotherapy, and in metastases derived from primary PDAC tumors with a mixed basal/ classical population. To create matched classical and basal cell lines, we stably transduced two classical PDAC cell lines (AsPC1 and HPAFII) with the basal program transcriptional driver ∆Np63α and assessed their growth, metastasis, and response to chemotherapy both in vitro and in vivo. Forced expression of ∆Np63α successfully converted both cell lines to basal transcriptomic subtype, yet the basal program failed to drive increased cell growth or chemoresistance in culture. Increased spontaneous pulmonary metastases of ∆Np63α+ HPAFII were seen in a murine orthotopic engraftment model, however, the metastases occurring from mixed control/ ∆Np63α+ tumors were not enriched for ∆Np63 expression, and ∆Np63α expression failed to increase tumor growth or metastasis in the AsPC1 model. Similarly, ∆Np63α+ HPAFII displayed increased resistance to irinotecan chemotherapy, yet treatment selected for ∆Np63-negative cells in both HPAFII and ASPC1. In summary, our data show that neither the metastatic cascade nor chemotherapy treatment preferentially select for basal PDAC.

title: Conserved cell state dynamics reveal targetable resistance patterns in ovarian high-grade serous carcinoma
summary: We characterized how the cell states of normal FTE are transformed into intra-tumoral heterogeneity in high-grade serous ovarian cancer (HGSC) using single-cell transcriptomics of treatment-naive tumors and normal FTE. Our cohort consists of scRNA-seq data from treatment-naïve HGSC tumor samples (n=52) and non-cancerous fallopian tube or fimbria tissue samples (n=7). After quality control, we obtained 131,225 cells, including 30,236 malignant epithelial, 1,251 secretory FTE, 80,764 immune and 18,974 stromal cells. Our study shows that conserved cell states reconstitute fallopian tube dynamics in HGSC and offer novel actionable targets to improve platinum response.

title: Cancer-Associated Fibroblast-Derived SOD3 Enhances Lymphangiogenesis to Drive Metastasis in Lung Adenocarcinoma
summary: Despite advancements in diagnostic and therapeutic strategies, lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) remains a leading cause of cancer-related mortality due to its aggressive metastatic potential. Extracellular superoxide dismutase (SOD3) is an antioxidant enzyme that regulates oxidative stress and is regarded as a tumor suppressor. However, studies have demonstrated that SOD3 can either promote or inhibit cell proliferation and survival in various cancers, and its molecular mechanisms within the tumor microenvironment are poorly understood. In this study, we report a breakthrough in uncovering the role of SOD3 derived from cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) in LUAD. Using LUAD xenograft models co-implanted with SOD3-overexpressing CAFs (CAFSOD3), we observe an aggressive tumor phenotype characterized by increased lymphangiogenesis and lymphatic vessel invasion (LVI) of the tumor. Additionally, LUAD patients with elevated SOD3 levels exhibit a higher incidence of LVI and metastasis. Notably, RNA sequencing of CAFSOD3 reveals that SOD3-mediated VEGF-dependent tumor progression and lymphangiogenesis are up-regulated. Furthermore, single-cell transcriptomic analysis of LUAD clinical samples confirms a strong correlation between SOD3 expression in fibroblasts and characteristics of tumor exacerbation, such as lymphangiogenesis and metastasis. These findings underscore new insights into the role of CAF-derived SOD3 in LUAD progression and highlight its potential as a biomarker and therapeutic target.

title: Gene expression analysis following GBM therapy INO-5104
summary: Glioblastoma (GBM) patients have not benefited from immune checkpoint therapy, largely due to a paucity of immune activated effector cells in the tumor microenvironment, highlighting the urgent need for novel strategies to improve patient outcomes. The combination of targeted DNA immunotherapy and checkpoint blockade has the potential to overcome this hurdle by stimulating a targeted immune response against tumor antigens and driving T cell infiltration into the glioblastomaGBM tumor microenvironment. We integrated a novel DNA-based immunotherapy strategy along with cemiplimab, a PD-1 inhibitor, into a backbone of hypofractionated radiation (RT) plus temozolomide chemotherapy (TMZ) in an open-label, single-arm, two-cohort Phase 1/ 2 clinical study with 52 eligible, newly diagnosed glioblastomaGBM patients, stratified by tumor methylguanine methyltransferase promoter methylation status: unmethylated (Cohort A) and methylated (Cohort B). The DNA immunotherapy, INO-5401, consisting of three plasmids each targeting tumor-associated antigens hTERT, WT-1, and PSMA, and an additional plasmid, INO-9012, encoding for IL-12, was administered via intramuscular injection followed by electroporation. The primary endpoint was safety; secondary endpoints included overall survival at 18 months (OS18), and antigen-specific cellular and humoral immune responses. TThe study regimen was well tolerated. 98% of patients experienced ≥1 treatment-emergent adverse eventsTEAE, most related to RT or TMZ and most wereprimarily Grade 1 or Grade 2. Overall survival at 18 months ( OS18) and median overall survival were 50% and 17.9 months for Cohort A and 70% and 32.9 months for Cohort B. Notably, patients exhibiting a peripheral immune response to INO-5401 antigens had a greater chance of survival at 18 months. Post hoc tumor analysis revealed increased immune cell activation and infiltration. INO-5401 + INO-9012 in combination with PD-1 blockade and hypofractionated chemo-radiotherapy induced treatment-reactive peripheral and intra-tumoral T cell expansion with an acceptable safety profile and encouraging survival in glioblastomaGBM patients. These findings underscore the potential of rationally designed DNA immunotherapy combinations to improve patient outcomes in glioblastomaGBM. ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT03491683

title: Nonopore sequencing of circRNAs and G3BP2-RIP sequencing in HCC827 cells
summary: Acquired resistance to third-generation EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) such as almonertinib presents a major clinical challenge in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Circular RNAs (circRNAs) are generated via back-splicing, and are versatile players in cancer biology. By using long-read nanopore sequencing, we profiled full-length circRNAs in almonertinib-resistant NSCLC cells and identified widespread alternative back-splicing (ABS) events in circRNAs. Among them, exon 3 of the PUM1 gene was a significantly regulated ABS exon, and led to the generation of most upregulated circRNA isoform of circPUM1(2-3) compared to circPUM1(2) in the resistant cells. Functional studies revealed that circPUM1(2-3) promoted cell viability and suppressed apoptosis by binding to the RNA-binding protein G3BP2 via its exon 3 sequences. This interaction competitively disrupted the G3BP2 binding to PSMA6 mRNA, which then increased the PSMA6 mRNA and protein levels, and led to the activation of MAPK/ERK pathway to promote cell survival.

title: IL-2Rα Overexpression Unlocks Enhanced CAR T Cell Persistence and Therapeutic Efficacy in B-Cell Lymphoma [RNA-seq]
summary: Interleukin-2 (IL-2) is critical for sustaining T cell expansion during infection and cancer. However, the high-affinity IL-2 receptor subunit IL-2Rα (CD25) is only transiently expressed following activation, limiting durable cytokine responsiveness. To overcome this barrier, we engineered CD19-directed CAR T cells with constitutive IL-2Rα expression and evaluated their functional fitness. CAR19-IL-2Rα T cells exhibited hypersensitive STAT5 signaling and proliferated more robustly than conventional CAR T cells under limiting IL-2 conditions. In long-term rechallenge assays, enforced IL-2Rα expression sustained proliferation, enhanced tumor clearance, and conferred resistance to regulatory T cell-mediated suppression by improving competition for IL-2. In a xenograft B cell lymphoma model, CAR19-IL-2Rα T cells improved tumor control and survival without increasing circulating cytokine levels associated with CRS or the expression of exhaustion-associated markers PD1 and LAG3. Transcriptomic profiling revealed strong induction of DDIT4, an mTORC1 inhibitor, following constitutive IL-2Rα expression in vivo, suggesting the activation of a feedback mechanism that limits CAR T cell expansion. Together, these results identify IL-2Rα overexpression as an engineering strategy that enhances CAR T cell function, improves resistance to regulatory T cell (Treg)-mediated immunosuppression, and promotes durable antitumor activity. This work establishes cytokine receptor rewiring as a simple and clinically compatible approach to enhance CAR T cell therapy in B-cell malignancies.

title: Novel Models of Group 4 Medulloblastoma for Accelerated Preclinical Discovery
summary: Background Medulloblastoma (MB) is the most common malignant pediatric brain tumor. MB is subdivided into four main subgroups: SHH, WNT, Group 3 (G3-MB) and Group 4 (G4-MB). Despite advancements in treatment regimens, 30% of MB patients succumb to tumor metastasis and treatment relapse. G4-MB represents a large subset of patients with poor prognosis. G4-MB tumor biology remains poorly understood and molecularly ambiguous. Pre-clinical development is obstructed by suboptimal existing models. here, we report the development of novel G4-MB models with the capacity for in vitro propagation and preclinical drug screening. Methods Two G4-MB tumor lines (MBT375 and MBT417) were derived from patient tumors and characterized by NanoString, RNA-seq and DNA methylation profiling. Subsequently, these models were serially engrafted in mice or cultured in vitro. G4MB models were assessed for stem cell marker BMI1 expression levels and subsequent dose-response and synergy assays were performed in comparison to normal neural stem cells with BMI1 targeted drugs. G4MB cells were transduced with firefly luciferase for optimized in vivo modelling. Results We present two novel G4-MB patient-derived orthotopic mouse models: MBT375 and MBT417, with the capacity for short-term in vitro propagation, genetic manipulation, and improved tumorigenicity. Importantly, MBT375-engrafted mice reliably develop spinal metastatic disease. By in vitro drug screening we demonstrate that repurposing G3-MB specific BMI1-targeted therapeutic strategies is a rational approach for the most common and often difficult-to-treat MB subtype. Conclusions We developed novel G4-MB models serving as in vitro discovery platforms to identify novel cancer-selective treatment modalities.

title: A case study using benzoic acid demonstrating how integration of in silico analogue selection tools with mechanistic in vitro NAM and toxicological data enhances the accuracy of RAX assessments of low systemic toxicity chemicals
summary: Benzoic acid and its related derivatives are preservatives widely used in the cosmetic and food industries. This study aimed to quantitatively assess the suitability of benzoic acid derivatives for read-across (RAX) in a Next Generation Risk Assessment. We employed in silico Matched Molecular Pair and Quantitative Similarity approaches to distinguish sub-groups within a broad category of benzoic acid-related substances. These were complemented with metabolism data to refine the category definitions. Pharmacology profiling, ToxCast and transcriptomic data further substantiated the low bioactivity of benzoic acid analogues and highlighted differences in reactivity for analogues outside the RAX category. Analogues with the highest TotalScore of 3.0 were salts of benzoic acid and p- and m-toluic acids, which exhibit similar metabolic pathways to benzoic acid. Small alkyl derivatives of benzoic acid exhibited slight metabolic differences, with TotalScores from <3.0 to ≥2.5. Based on the RAX evaluation, the category of benzoates using benzoic acid as a source of toxicological data included the sodium, potassium, calcium, magnesium and ammonium salts of benzoic acid and m- and p-toluic acid. Physiologically Based Kinetic modelling was used to better understand the discordance of in vivo toxicity data due to the administration route, and the lack of bioactivity of benzoic acid and its analogues in in vitro tests. In conclusion, this case study illustrates a structured approach to evaluating the suitability and safety of analogues and demonstrates the utility of integrating in silico tools with mechanistic and toxicological data to enhance the accuracy of RAX assessments.

title: Inhibition of a corrupted embryonic developmental regulator reverses colon cancer to a normal-like state [TAF10_bulk_RNA]
summary: Reverting cancer cells into a normal-like state offers a therapeutic alternative to eliminating malignant cells. This raises questions about the existence and possible identification of a molecular switch that governs such reversion. We analyzed single-cell transcriptomes from patient-derived paired colon organoids, integrating copy number alterations to delineate a transition state between normal and malignant cells. Regulatory network analysis of this state identified TAF10 as a reversion switch whose knockdown drives colorectal cancer cells toward a normal-like state, without effecting normal cell growth. Logical network modeling predicted that TAF10 knockdown suppresses oncogenic WNT, mTOR, and MAPK signaling, while activating enterocyte differentiation. Consistent with these predictions, organoid and in vivo assays demonstrated reduced malignancy and increased differentiation. Although TAF10 is essential for embryonic development and appears insignificant once silenced in adult tissues, colorectal cancer reactivates it through interaction with the SAGA complex, hijacking a developmental program whose control exposes a therapeutic vulnerability.

title: ALKR1275Q expands Schwann Cell Precursor-like cells during sympathoadrenal commitment, creating a permissive state for neuroblastoma initiation.
summary: Neuroblastoma (NB) is a pediatric malignancy developing in the sympathoadrenal lineage of the neural crest, characterized by clinical heterogeneity ranging from spontaneous regression to poor outcomes. Activating mutations in the receptor tyrosine kinase anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK) are frequently observed in both sporadic and familial NB, yet the functional role of ALK in tumor initiation is not fully understood. Using a patient-derived human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) model of sympathoadrenal development, we show that upon sympathoadrenal lineage commitment, ALK R1275Q, the most common hotspot mutation found in familial NB, sustain a proliferative, immature Schwann cell precursor (SCP)-like cell state with elevated ALK signaling and increased susceptibility to MYCN-driven transformation. While ALK-mutant cells alone did not form tumors in vivo, they cooperated with MYCN to accelerate tumor initiation, suggesting that ALK R1275Q creates a permissive but insufficient state for transformation. These findings define an ALK-driven cell progenitor-like state that facilitates the initiation of NB during embryonal development.

title: Complementary single-nucleus and single-cell RNA sequencing reveal tumor state evolution and microenvironmental rewiring in NSCLC
summary: Single-cell (scRNA-seq) and single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) provide complementary strategies for profiling complex tissues, but differ in RNA content, cell-type representation and transcript coverage. Here, we perform a direct comparison of matched tumor and adjacent normal tissues from patients with non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), integrating in-house and public datasets to delineate platform-specific strengths and limitations. Both platforms recovered major cellular compartments with high fidelity: scRNA-seq showed greater sensitivity for immune populations, whereas snRNA-seq captured epithelial, endothelial and fibroblast lineages more effectively. Comparative transcriptomic profiling of shared cell types uncovered distinct yet coherent functional programs: snRNA-seq emphasized nuclear RNA processing and proteostasis, while scRNA-seq enriched for mitochondrial respiration and translational pathways. Integrative regulon of alveolar differentiation and tumor progression revealed coordinated transcriptional regulators (FOXP2, STAT3, MEF2A, FOXO3) governing the AT2-to-AT1 trajectory and divergent gene programs associated with AT2-to-malignant transition. Ligand-receptor mapping further uncovered platform-specific intercellular signaling, with snRNA-seq highlighting matrix- and TGF-ß – driven stromal interactions and scRNA-seq revealing angiogeneic and immune-regulatory pathways. Collectively, this study defines complementary modalities for dissecting epithelial dynamics and tumor communication in NSCLC.

title: Translational profiling of ET-insensitive cell populations in ER+ breast cancer reveals new therapeutic vulnerabilities [scRNA-Seq]
summary: Endocrine therapy resistance in ER+ breast cancer remains a major therapeutic challenge in clinic. This study offers a robust workflow to identify ET-insensitive cell populations that persist under selective pressure of ET in clinical samples and experimental models. We demonstrated that these populations are transcriptionally diverse and not defined by ER status/activity or molecular subtype. Importantly, we developed a predictive therapeutic pipeline that enables identification of new drugs tailored to target ET-insensitive cell populations. These findings provide a clinically relevant strategy for overcoming ET resistance and support the integration of single-cell profiling and organoid modeling into precision oncology workflows.

title: Matrix Stiffness-Induced YEATS2 Drives HCC Progression via Epigenetic Activation of the TGFBR2-TAZ-AKT Pathway
summary: YEATS2, a crucial component of histone acetyltransferase (HAT) complexes, is found to be overexpressed in various human malignancies and is associated with tumor progression and poor patient prognoses. However, its specific role in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) remains to be clarified. This study aims to investigate the function and mechanisms by which YEATS2 facilitates HCC growth and metastasis. Our results indicate that YEATS2 expression is significantly elevated in HCC tissues and correlates with adverse clinical characteristics and decreased survival rates. Functional assays demonstrate that YEATS2 enhances HCC cell proliferation, migration, and invasion in both in vitro and in vivo models. RNA sequencing and mass spectrometry analyses reveal that YEATS2 activates the TAZ/AKT signaling pathway and promotes aerobic glycolysis through the upregulation of TGFBR2. Chromatin immunoprecipitation and co-immunoprecipitation assays further confirm that YEATS2 interacts with KAT2A, resulting in increased levels of H3K9ac and H3K14ac in the promoter region of TGFBR2, thereby augmenting its transcription. Additionally, increased matrix stiffness was found to elevate YEATS2 expression through enhanced the binding of HIF-1α at the YEATS2 promoter. Collectively, our findings delineate a novel YEATS2-TGFBR2-TAZ-AKT signaling axis that links matrix stiffness to metabolic reprogramming and the progression of HCC, suggesting a potential therapeutic target for the treatment of HCC.

title: Engineered in vitro microvascular model of the blood-brain-tumor barrier to probe vascular biology of pediatric diffuse midline glioma
summary: Diffuse midline glioma (DMG) is a highly aggressive pediatric brain tumor that is difficult to treat because the blood-brain-tumor barrier (BBTB) prevents most drugs from reaching the tumor. A major obstacle for understanding this tumor-vascular niche is the lack of a perfusable vascular model of DMG. To address this, we have established an in vitro model of the DMG-BBTB, comprised of a co-culture of patient-derived DMG tumor cells, primary human brain microvascular endothelial cells, astrocytes, and vascular pericytes, embedded in a fibrin matrix within a microfluidic chip. We report the development and characterization of self-assembled microvascular networks, with consistent vasculature development across a range of tumor cell densities. Perfusion studies showed no significant alterations in vascular permeability when tumor cells were present. To elucidate transcriptomic changes, we employed scRNAseq on devices containing BBB, DMG-BBTB, or tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNFα)-stimulated control. We observed significant differential gene expression between BBB and DMG-BBTB, distinct from inflammatory signatures seen with TNFα perturbation. Our analysis indicated that DMG cells adopted a mesenchymal-like phenotype, with further in silico studies predicting significant receptor-ligand crosstalk between these cells and endothelium. In summary, we developed a high-fidelity DMG-BBTB model that recapitulates the transcriptomic features of patient DMG microvasculature and features perfusable vasculature that enables functional testing of therapeutics.

title: Targeting SOST-LRRC15 axis impairs triple-negative breast cancer progression by regulating Wnt signaling and EMT
summary: Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) remains a therapeutic challenge due to its aggressive nature and lack of targeted therapies. While Sclerostin (SOST) is a well-established Wnt antagonist in bone metabolism, its role in cancer pathogenesis is poorly understood. Here, we identify SOST as a context-dependent oncoprotein in TNBC and delineate a novel pathogenic axis. Analysis of TCGA data revealed the expression of SOST is highly upregulated in TNBC and correlates with poor patient survival. Functional studies demonstrated that SOST drives TNBC cell proliferation, migration, and invasion. Mechanistically, transcriptomic analyses revealed that SOST activates Wnt/β-catenin signaling and epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) programs-a paradoxical function opposite to its canonical role. Through co-immunoprecipitation-mass spectrometry, we identified LRRC15 as a key SOST-binding partner that facilitates its secretion. The SOST-LRRC15 interaction was validated both biochemically and clinically, with co-expression predicting poor prognosis. Furthermore, therapeutic targeting of SOST using either a specific aptamer or the small molecule inhibitor SOSTi effectively suppressed TNBC malignancy in vitro. Our findings establish a novel SOST-LRRC15 regulatory axis that promotes TNBC progression through coordinated activation of Wnt signaling and EMT, positioning SOST as a promising therapeutic target for this aggressive breast cancer subtype.

title: Gene expression data for pathological stage I-II lung adenocarcinomas
summary: Identification of genes up-regulated in ALK-positive and EGFR/KRAS/ALK-negative lung adenocarcinomas. To elucidate molecular characteristics of lung adenocarcinomas (ADCs) with ALK mutations and those without EGFR, KRAS and ALK mutations, 226 primary lung ADCs of pathological stage I-II, examined for the status of EGFR, KRAS and ALK mutations, were subjected to genome-wide expression profiling, and genes up-regulated in lung ADCs with ALK mutations and those without EGFR, KRAS and ALK mutations were identified. One hundred and seventy-four genes, including ALK, were selected as being up-regulated specifically in 79 lung ADCs without EGFR and KRAS mutations. These 79 cases were divided into: 11 cases of ALK-positive ADCs, 36 cases of group A triple-negative ADCs, and 32 cases of group B triple-negative ADCs, by unsupervised clustering according to the expression of the 174 genes. In ALK-positive ADCs, 30 genes, including ALK itself and GRIN2A, were significantly overexpressed. Group A triple-negative ADC cases showed significantly worse prognoses for relapse and death than ADC cases with EGFR, KRAS or ALK mutations and group B triple-negative ADC cases. Nine genes were identified as being significantly up-regulated in group A triple-negative ADC cases and critical for predicting their prognosis. The nine genes included DEPDC1, which had been identified as a candidate diagnostic and therapeutic target in bladder and breast cancers. Genes discriminating this group of ADCs will be useful for selection of patients who will benefit from adjuvant chemotherapy after surgical resection of stage I-II triple-negative ADCs and also informative for the development of molecular targeting therapies for these patients.

title: Cell-type-specific transcriptomic programs induced by progesterone and bazedoxifene to prevent estradiol-driven proliferation in the human endometrium
summary: Menopausal hormone therapy (MHT) combining estrogen with a progestogen protects the endometrium in non-hysterectomized women but increases breast cancer risk, prompting the search for progestogen-free alternatives. Selective estrogen receptor modulators (SERMs), such as bazedoxifene (BZA), offer a potential solution, yet their use for menopausal indications remains debated. MHT evaluations rely largely on mouse models or clinical measurements of endometrial thickness, providing limited mechanistic insight in human tissue. Here, we performed cell-type-specific transcriptomic profiling of patient-derived endometrial xenografts to compare how progesterone and BZA prevent estradiol-induced proliferation. Both treatments act through specific mechanisms: progesterone preserves half of the estradiol-dependent transcriptional response while inducing new programs, whereas BZA broadly abrogates estradiol-driven signaling in epithelial and stromal cells. We further identified cell-specific transcription factors and differential regulation of paracrine/autocrine networks. Overall, this study provides mechanistic and transcriptomic resources from human endometrium, with important implications for the development of improved MHT strategies.

title: Development of Novel EGLN2-Selective Small Molecule Inhibitor for Breast cancer
summary: The development of isoform-selective EGLN2 inhibitors remains a major challenge and an important opportunity in cancer therapeutics. Here, we report the discovery of A10P3C, a novel small-molecule inhibitor that exhibits high potency and exceptional selectivity toward EGLN2. Guided by conformational sampling and ensemble-docking-based pharmacophore analysis, which indicated strategic chemical modifications to an initially screened lead compound, A10P3C was rationally designed to engage the unique structural features of the EGLN2 catalytic pocket. Unlike previously reported pan-hydroxylase inhibitors, A10P3C achieves unprecedented isoform selectivity. Functionally, A10P3C effectively suppresses breast cancer cell proliferation, migration, and invasion, while inducing G1 cell cycle arrest and cellular senescence through on-target EGLN2 inhibition. These on-target effects are corroborated by transcriptomic profiling, which shows significant modulation of cell cycle and senescence pathways. Notably, A10P3C exhibits robust anti-tumor efficacy in patient-derived organoids and xenograft models, accompanied by favorable metabolic stability and minimal systemic toxicity. Collectively, these findings identify A10P3C as a novel and selective chemical probe for EGLN2 biology and a promising therapeutic lead for precision treatment of EGLN2-driven breast cancers.

title: Adaptive ACK1 depletion drives IL-8-mediated HER2 loss and therapeutic resistance in breast cancer
summary: HER2-amplified breast cancers benefit from dual HER2 blockade with trastuzumab and pertuzumab in both neoadjuvant and advanced settings, yet intratumoral HER2 heterogeneity and adaptive resistance limit therapeutic efficacy. Here, we identify a mechanism of “adaptive oncogene loss,” in which resistant cells downregulate the non-receptor tyrosine kinase ACK1 to suppress HER2 expression and evade therapy. Transcriptomic profiling of resistant HER2-positive cell models and patient datasets, combined with functional assays including siRNA, overexpression, chromatin immunoprecipitation, and high-content immunofluorescence, revealed that prolonged dual HER2 blockade reduces ACK1 levels, unleashing a STAT1/STAT3-dependent transcriptional repression of ERBB2 via proximal and distal regulatory elements. This process is sustained by an autocrine IL-8/JAK/STAT and further amplified by exogenous IL-6, resulting in decreased membrane HER2 and impaired sensitivity to HER2-targeted antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs). Elevated cytokine signaling correlates with reduced HER2 in patient datasets, and pharmacologic inhibition of JAK/STAT restores HER2 expression and ADC sensitivity in resistant models. These findings establish adaptive oncogene loss as a mechanism of HER2-targeted therapy resistance and highlight the IL-6/IL-8-JAK/STAT axis as a therapeutically actionable pathway to restore HER2 expression and improve outcomes in HER2-positive breast cancer.

title: Transcriptomic profiling of A549 lung adenocarcinoma cells treated with natural killer cell-derived exosomes reveals pyroptosis-related ceRNA networks_mRNAseq+lncRNA
summary: Lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) remains a challenging malignancy with limited treatment options. Natural killer (NK) cell-derived exosomes have emerged as a promising anti-cancer therapeutic approach. To investigate the transcriptomic mechanisms underlying NK exosome-induced cytotoxicity in LUAD, we performed comprehensive RNA sequencing of A549 human LUAD cells treated with exosomes isolated from NK92 human NK cells (NK92-exo) versus untreated controls. This dataset includes mRNA and miRNA expression profiles from NK92-exo-treated and control A549 cells after 72 hours of treatment. This transcriptomic resource provides insights into the molecular mechanisms of NK exosome-induced anti-tumor effects and identifies potential therapeutic targets for LUAD treatment.

title: Pitavastatin counteracts venetoclax resistance mechanisms including TP53 mutation in acute myeloid leukemia I
summary: The BCL2 inhibitor venetoclax has therapeutic activity in several hematological malignancies. In acute myeloid leukemia (AML), venetoclax combined with hypomethylating agents is the standard of care for patients unfit for intensive chemotherapy, but intrinsic and acquired resistance are common. Loss of p53 function is strongly associated with venetoclax resistance, and adding venetoclax to 5-azacitidine provides no overall survival benefit in TP53-mutant AML. Other frequent mechanisms of venetoclax resistance in AML include FLT3 mutations, MCL-1 upregulation, and altered mitochondrial metabolism. Unfortunately, it has been challenging to develop agents that target these mechanisms directly and combinatorially. Here we report that pitavastatin, an inhibitor of HMG-CoA-reductase, promotes apoptosis and overcomes several venetoclax resistance mechanisms in human AML cells. At clinically achievable concentrations, pitavastatin treatment has potent cytotoxic activity in cells with mutations in TP53 or FLT3. The apoptotic mechanism involves p53-independent PUMA upregulation and reduced MCL-1 expression. Pitavastatin also suppresses mitochondrial gene expression and oxidative metabolism. The pro-apoptotic actions of pitavastatin depend on depletion of geranylgeranyl pyrophosphate (GGPP) and can be recapitulated by inhibiting GGPP synthase or geranylgeranyltransferase-1 enzymes. These results provide a mechanistic rationale for adding pitavastatin to AML regimens to prevent or overcome venetoclax resistance.

title: FOXA1 promotes SCLC chemoresistance [RNA-Seq]
summary: Small cell lung cancer (SCLC) is an aggressive neuroendocrine tumor. While chemotherapy has been the cornerstone of first-line treatment, most SCLC patients develop chemoresistance shortly after an initial response, and the molecular basis of this resistance remains poorly understood. Here, we identify FOXA1 as a frequently amplified and upregulated gene in SCLC, with high FOXA1 expression correlating with poor outcomes. We further demonstrate that FOXA1 overexpression promotes resistance to chemotherapy. Mechanistically, we reveal that WNT5A is a downstream target of FOXA1 that mediates chemoresistance through activation of the Wnt/β-catenin pathway. FOXA1 also induces epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) in SCLC cells, and human SCLC tumors with high FOXA1 expression exhibit enriched EMT and Wnt/β-catenin pathway signatures. Importantly, pharmacological inhibition of the Wnt pathway selectively suppresses the growth of FOXA1-overexpressing SCLC cells. Collectively, our study identifies FOXA1 as a key driver of chemoresistance in SCLC and highlights Wnt pathway inhibition as a promising strategy to overcome FOXA1-driven chemoresistance.

title: Kinome-profiling enabled discovery of a LATS1/2 inhibitor with wound healing potential
summary: System-level mapping of kinase inhibitors’ polypharmacology can uncover opportunities for drug repurposing and identify starting points for medicinal chemistry campaigns aimed at novel targets. Here, we describe a large-scale profiling of 257 kinase inhibitors that revealed domains of promiscuity, pockets of selectivity, and a broad region of uninhibited targets. Focusing on a subcluster enriched for AGC group kinases and using the AKT inhibitor AT-7867 (an antiproliferative agent) as a starting point, we employed scaffold hopping and property-based optimization to discover NCGC-6782, a LATS1/2 inhibitor with robust pro-proliferative activity. In cells, NCGC-6782 inhibited LATS1/2 activity, promoted rapid YAP nuclear translocation and transactivation of YAP-target genes. Kinome-wide profilings demonstrated good in vitro selectivity and exquisite chemoproteomic and kinetic selectivity. Transcriptomics and proteomics following NCGC-6782 revealed upregulation of YAP-dependent genes (4h) followed by activation of cell cycle programs (24h). Consistently, NCGC-6782 accelerated proliferative regeneration in both cell-based and in vivo wound healing models

title: The mitochondrial chaperone HSPD1 folds MTHFD2 independently of its co-chaperone HSPE1 [A549 HSPD1 KD]
summary: Acquiring new cellular states entails metabolic reprogramming driven by adjustments to the expression of metabolic enzymes in the cytosol and mitochondria. Most mitochondrial proteins are synthesized in the cytosol and imported into the mitochondria in a linear form, after which they are folded by a network of mitochondrial chaperones and co-chaperones. Which mitochondrial protein is dependent upon which chaperone for its folding is largely unknown. HSPD1/HSPE1 (HSP60/HSP10) are evolutionarily conserved mammalian homologues of bacterial proteins GroEL/GroES, forming a chamber and lid chaperonin to facilitate folding of their client proteins. We used gene knockdown and SILAC-based proteomics to identify HSPD1 client proteins. We found that HSPD1 supports the expression of MTHFD2, a key mitochondrial one-carbon (1C) enzyme, in vivo and folds MTHFD2 in vitro, independently of its co-chaperone HSPE1. HSPD1 interacts with MTHFD2 in mitochondria, and MTHFD2 is degraded by LONP in HSPD1 knockdown cells. Consequently, we found reduced nucleotide and SAM levels in HSPD1 knockdown and found little overlap in the transcriptional or metabolic response to HSPD1 vs. HSPE1 depletion. Our data support that specific chaperones cater to the folding of specific proteins in the mitochondria and that HSPD1 and HSPE1 have distinct biological functions.

title: A non-canonical role for E2F1 in driving the development of neuroendocrine prostate cancer.
summary: Collective data support neuroendocrine prostate cancer (NEPC) arising as a mechanism of resistance to anti-androgen receptor (AR) therapy, with tumors losing AR protein expression and/or canonical AR signaling and acquiring alternative lineage programs to drive growth and histologic transformation. Though sharing histologic and molecular features with small cell lung cancer (such as TP53 mutations and retinoblastoma tumor suppressor gene (RB1) loss), NEPC retains many of the early genomic alterations that arise in prostate adenocarcinoma. Canonically, RB1 controls cell cycle progression by binding to E2F1, preventing E2F1-mediated cell cycle genes expression. Here, we show that E2F1 is overexpressed in NEPC and a subset of CRPC patient tumors and associated with poor prognosis. E2F1 overexpression in prostate adenocarcinoma cells is correlated with the NEPC-associated transcriptional program, while E2F1 depletion reverses E2F1-associated repression of AR signaling and induction of NEPC-associated gene expression. E2F1 interacts with and co-localizes with FOXA2 at active regulatory elements of key NEPC-associated genes and induces INSM1 expression in models of advanced prostate cancer. E2F1 depletion in established NEPC cells decreases the transcriptional repression of neural lineage-associated genes by RE1 silencing transcription factor (REST). Altogether, our data shows that E2F1 plays a non-canonical role in driving a NEPC-associated change in gene expression and which is mediated through a physical interaction with specific NEPC-associated co-factors and transcription factors.

title: NSCLC KRAS G12C MUTANT CELLS ARE DEPENDENT ON MUC1-C FOR RESISTANCE TO KRAS INHIBITORS II
summary: Treatment of NSCLC KRAS G12C mutant tumors with targeted KRAS inhibitors, such as sotorasib and adagrasib, is invariably associated with the emergence of acquired resistance. We report that patients with NSCLC KRAS G12C tumors expressing increased levels of the MUC1 gene exhibit decreases in overall survival in response to sotorasib and adagrasib. Studies of sotorasib-resistant (SR) cells further reveal upregulation of M1C chromatin levels in association with activation of the epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT). Mechanistically, M1C drives NF-kB p65-mediated induction of the ZEB1 EMT-TF. Furthermore, targeting M1C NF-kB ZEB1 signaling suppresses EMT and sotorasib resistance. Having identified this M1C dependence, we demonstrate that targeting M1C with an antibody-drug conjugate (ADC) is effective against sotorasib-resistant cells growing in vitro and as tumor xenografts. These findings identify M1C as a major effector of sotorasib resistance and as a target for ADC treatment of patients with refractory NSCLC KRAS G12C mutant tumors.

title: Vascular smooth muscle cell abundance is a hallmark of Castleman Disease
summary: Castleman Disease (CD) is a poorly understood inflammatory disorder characterized by enlarged lymph nodes with distinctive histologic features. Its opaque pathophysiology delays diagnoses and limits treatments, leading to additional morbidity and mortality. Since lymph nodes are the key lesional tissue for the disease, we sought to better understand the molecular and cellular underpinnings of CD lymph nodes using single cell and spatial transcriptomics. We found pronounced alterations in cell composition and dysregulation of distinct molecular pathways in non-hematopoietic stromal cells in lymph nodes from the unicentric form of CD. In contrast, hematopoietic cells in CD lymph nodes showed only few compositional or expression changes when compared to enlarged lymph nodes with non-specific inflammation. The elevated abundance of vascular smooth muscle cells, a subset of lymph node stromal cells, in unicentric CD lymph nodes and broadly increased stromal cell activity signified CD lymph nodes. In particular, immunohistochemical staining for the vascular smooth muscle cell marker CD146 (Melanoma Cell Adhesion Molecule, MCAM) served as reliable discriminator of unicentric CD lymph nodes from related lymphadenopathies. In sum, single cell and spatial transcriptomic analyses of CD lymph nodes facilitate the identification of CD-specific molecular and cellular features to guide diagnosis and patient stratification.

title: Immune and Cellular Determinants of Response to HMA-Venetoclax Regimens in Acute Myeloid Leukemia
summary: Hypomethylating agents (HMAs) combined with Venetoclax have redefined the therapeutic landscape of acute myeloid leukemia (AML), yet the biological underpinnings of treatment response remain elusive. We integrated clinical and genomic profiling in 132 patients with newly diagnosed or relapsed/refractory AML treated with HMA-Venetoclax. Additionally, we performed single-cell RNA sequencing and T cell receptor (TCR) profiling at baseline and after one cycle in 10 newly diagnosed cases to dissect cell-intrinsic and immune determinants of response. Response rates and overall survival were consistent with published data, supporting HMA-Venetoclax as a valid bridge to transplant. Targeted next-generation sequencing delineated molecular subgroups, confirming the favorable impact of IDH2 and the poor prognosis associated with TP53 mutations. scRNAseq and TCR analysis revealed novel immune correlates: responders showed expansion of cytotoxic CD8⁺ T cells, increased TCR clonality, and activation of inflammatory and antigen presentation pathways. Non-responders exhibited baseline inflammatory signaling (Interferon, NF-κB), impaired myeloid maturation via NOTCH and RAS, and a suppressive microenvironment enriched in IDO1⁺ regulatory dendritic cells. Resistant AMLs, especially those with TP53 and RAS mutations, underwent transcriptional dedifferentiation toward stem-like states and sustained epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT), indicating lineage plasticity. T cell analysis revealed divergent clonal dynamics: responders showed cytotoxic remodeling of CD4⁺ and CD8⁺ populations, while non-responders retained dysfunctional phenotypes marked by persistent LAG-3 expression. Our findings uncover previously unrecognized cellular states and resistance trajectories in AML treated with HMA-Venetoclax, and idenitfy LAG-3 as a possible biomarker of response and a rational target for immunotherapeutic intervention.

title: Mechanistic Language Modeling and Oxygenated 3D Screening Reveal Berberine and Enzalutamide Synergy in Resistant Prostate Cancer
summary: Resistance to androgen receptor inhibitors remains a primary challenge in prostate cancer treatment, yet identifying synergistic co-therapies is hindered by immense combinatorial search spaces and the limited interpretability of predictive computation models. Here, we developed an integrated discovery-validation axis coupling knowledge-augmented large language models with oxygen-supplemented 3D spheroid assays. By leveraging inherent model stochasticity, our framework measures the degree of consensus across independent predictions to establish a formal metric for predictive accuracy. This principle enables high-throughput assessment of complex signaling crosstalk, yielding mechanistic rationales for all predictions and defining a high-confidence zone that minimizes experimental attrition. Utilizing this approach to screen 3,592 natural products, we identified a previously unrecognized synergy between berberine and enzalutamide that re-sensitizes resistant cells. Validation confirms that berberine perturbs the PI3K/AKT/mTOR and AMPK axes, a finding consistent with the mechanistic rationales computationally derived by the framework. Integrating interpretable AI with physiologically relevant 3D screening provides a scalable methodology for the rational discovery of synergistic therapies.

title: Single-cell transcriptomics of peripheral blood reveals race-associated gene expression divergence in breast cancer from precancerous stages
summary: Black women more likely develop breast cancer at younger ages compared with other populations, yet reasons behind are not fully understood. As the immune system influences cancer development and progression, we hypothesized that immune differences by race could reflect underlying mechanisms. Here, we developed a single-cell transcriptomic PBMC atlas, including samples from Non-Hispanic Black patients with high-risk breast lesions, DCIS, and invasive breast cancer and compared them with Non-Hispanic White patients. PBMC composition varied modestly by disease state and race, whereas transcriptomic divergence was pronounced. Differential expression analysis showed that transcriptomic diverges in invasive disease from precancer states, and that race-associated transcriptomic difference was also strongest in invasive breast cancer. Covarying neighborhood analysis and pathway analysis identified race/ethnicity-associated pathways enriched in NHB, featuring pathways linked to chronic inflammation, immune suppression, and immune aging in monocytes, dendritic cells, CD4+ T cells, and B cells. This dataset is a valuable resource characterizing peripheral immune changes during breast cancer development from racially/ethnically inclusive populations.

title: ACSS2-Mediated Metabolic-Epigenetic Crosstalk Drives Fulvestrant Resistance and Represents a Novel Therapeutic Target
summary: Endocrine therapies target hormone-dependent cancer cells, primarily through estrogen receptor alpha (ERα), expressed in ~70% of breast cancers (ER+). Despite treatment advances, 30-40% of ER+ breast cancer patients experience recurrence and metastasis, with 5-year survival rates of only 31.9%. We validated poor outcomes for liver metastasis patients treated with Fulvestrant (Fulv) using the local Carle Foundation Hospital cohort and examined metabolic pathways in liver metastatic patient-derived xenograft (PDX) models, revealing upregulated lipid and acetyl-CoA production. Our previous work demonstrated that combining Fulv with acetyl-CoA synthase inhibitor (ACSI) targeting Acyl-CoA Synthetase Short Chain Family Member 2 (ACSS2), synergistically reduced ER+ metastatic breast cancer (MBC) cell viability in vitro. Using multiple analytical approaches-isotope tracing, CUT&RUN sequencing, immunofluorescence, western blot, and RNA sequencing-we characterized the effects of acetyl-CoA synthesis inhibition on Fulv-induced alterations. Fulv treatment of MBC cells increased ACSS2 expression and acetate utilization. Isotope tracing revealed that Fulv decreased acetate flux to the TCA cycle while promoting fatty acid synthesis. Importantly, ACSS2 was predominantly nuclear and CUT&RUN sequencing showed that Fulv treatment increased ACSS2 chromatin occupancy and ERα/ACSS2/H3K27ac overlapping sites near genes associated with tumor progression, which was eliminated by combination of ACSI and Fulv. RNA sequencing revealed reduction of Fulv-induced expression of genes involved in cancer cell metabolism and key signaling pathways in cancer with the Fulv+ACSI combination. In a therapy-resistant xenograft model, combining Fulv and ACSI reduced Fulv-dependent increase in metastatic burden. Our findings indicate ACSS2 contributes to endocrine therapy resistance through nuclear acetyl-CoA provision for epigenetic alterations. Targeting these cancer cell adaptations represents a novel therapeutic approach potentially reducing metastasis-related mortality and improving breast cancer treatment outcomes.

title: Elevated miR-103b in exosomes derived from brain-metastatic triple-negative breast cancer cells remodels the brain pre-metastatic niche (PMN)
summary: Triple-Negative Breast Cancer (TNBC) is a highly aggressive breast cancer with high brain metastatic potential. Tumor-derived exosomes have been indicated as key drivers for tumor metastasis owing to their ability to modulate the pre-metastatic niche (PMN). However, the regulation of TNBC-BM-derived exosomes on brain PMN remains enigmatic. Here, we found that miR-103b was significantly increased in exosomes derived from MDA-MB-231Brm cells. miR-103b compromised the tight junction of HUVECs and increased permeability of the BBB in mice. Additionally, miR-103b promoted apoptosis and elevated intracellular ROS in HUVECs and U-251 cells, two cell lines homologous to brain microvascular endothelial cells (BMECs) and astrocytes, respectively. High-throughput RNA-sequencing and bioinformatics analysis demonstrated that miR-103b-regulated differentially expressed genes (DEGs) modulated tight junction, cell cycle, apoptosis, oxidative stress, inflammation, and metabolism in HUVECs and U-251 cells. Target analysis revealed 216 targets of miR-103b and the hub targets were associated with the biological process of maintenance of the BBB and glucose metabolism signaling pathway. Collectively, our findings for the first time reveal the potential regulation of miR-103b on the BMECs and astrocytes, highlighting the role of miR-103b in the formation of brain PMN during TNBC-BM and its potential as a promising therapeutic target.

title: Optogenetic Modeling of Wake-Like Transcriptional Progression in Human SH-SY5Y Neuronal Cells
summary: Sleep deprivation induces extensive transcriptional remodeling in the brain, yet it remains unclear how much of this response arises directly from sustained neuronal excitation versus systemic and behavioral confounds. Here we establish a reductionist human neuronal cell model to isolate the cell-autonomous consequences of prolonged depolarization. Controlled optogenetic stimulation of human SH-SY5Y neuronal cells elicited scalable calcium influx and robust induction of canonical activity-dependent genes, enabling precise manipulation of excitation history independent of receptor-specific pleiotropy. Time-resolved RNA sequencing revealed that sustained excitation does not produce a uniform transcriptional shift. Instead, responses partitioned into a small set of reproducible temporal modules including early-, mid-, and late-peaking induction, sustained induction, biphasic responses, and suppression, each associated with distinct functional and regulatory signatures. At the systems level, pathway activities evolved through three sequential transcriptional states, each defined by a distinct mixture of these temporal gene modules within individual programs. State transitions were directional and asymmetric across stimulation and recovery, consistent with cumulative excitation-history–dependent reorganization rather than simple reversal after stimulus offset. Cross-dataset mapping with in vivo mouse sleep datasets showed selective concordance between defined temporal modules and independent sleep-deprivation signatures. Together, these findings show that sustained neuronal excitation alone is sufficient to generate staged, wake-like transcriptional progression, linking gene-level temporal structure to higher-order regulatory states shaped by excitation history.

title: Single-Nucleus Analysis of NF1 Low-Grade Glioma Tumoroids Reveals a Metabolic Shift and Myeloid Evolution In Vitro
summary: About 10-15% of individuals with Neurofibromatosis Type 1 develop a low-grade glioma (LGG) within the optic pathway, and an additional 3-5% of individuals develop LGG outside of the optic pathway. In recent years molecular analysis has greatly enhanced our understanding of what drives these NF1 LGG; however, to date in vitro models are rare and in vivo models are scarce. Here, we present the first in vitro tumor-derived spheroid cultures (tumoroids) of 3 NF1-associated LGGs grown for up to 4 weeks. These tumoroids can be passaged and banked. To determine how accurately the NF1 LGG tumoroid cultures reflect human disease, and how much and how quickly they drift from the primary tumors, we performed single nuclear RNAseq (snRNAseq) analysis on primary tumor and 1, 2 and 4 weeks in culture for one of these NF1 LGG tumoroid lines. Observations were confirmed with immunofluorescence staining on all 3 NF1 LGG tumoroid lines. As expected, the few CD3+ T-cells present in the primary tumor are lost by day 14 (IF) and not detected on scRNAseq; macrophages/microglia remain present for at least 14 days but are largely depleted by week 4. Additionally, we observe a shift from more homeostatic microglia in the primary tumor to CD163 positive tumor-associated macrophages/microglia (TAM) in vitro. Neoplastic clusters uniquely associated with the primary tumor had clear upregulation of genes associated with neuronal communication. Our analysis also shows that primary NF1 LGGs rely on the metabolism of fatty acids (FA) for energy, while in vitro, glycolysis is the primary energy source. Additionally, instead of metabolizing FA, both neoplastic and immune cells switch to FA synthesis in vitro. Finally, we observe a slightly increased proliferative index in vitro versus in vivo, both in neoplastic and immune cells. Given the paucity of in vitro models, NF1-derived tumoroids, open opportunities for screening drug sensitivity and other studies.
