title: Compartment-Resolved Profiling Identifies Shared Stromal Programs and Clarifies Molecular Subtype Origins in Ovarian Cancer [RNA-seq]
summary: Epithelial ovarian cancers (EOCs) comprise biologically distinct histotypes that arise within shared anatomical niches where tumor-stroma interactions shape tumor behavior and therapeutic response. However, whether different histotypes engage common stromal programs, and how stromal signals influence canonical molecular subtypes remain unclear, as most classification frameworks rely on bulk profiling that conflates epithelial and stromal contributions. Here, we performed compartment-resolved transcriptomic and epigenomic profiling of matched carcinoma and stroma across clear cell (CCOC), endometrioid (ENOC), and high-grade serous ovarian cancers (HGSC). Carcinoma profiles segregated strongly by histotype, whereas stromal profiles showed minimal histotype specificity and instead resolved into four shared groups (S1–S4). The S4 subtype, marked by a desmoplastic, myofibroblast-rich program, was enriched in omental tumors and corresponded to the HGSC C1/Mesenchymal signature. We show this subtype likely reflects tumor-extrinsic programs and is present beyond HGSC. Compartment-resolved analyses also clarify other molecular carcinoma subtypes and reveal carcinoma-intrinsic EMT programs.

title: MYC-ATF4-ASS1 axis governs intracellular arginine synthesis and dictates the immune microenvironment in melanoma [Bulk RNA-seq]
summary: Drug resistance is a major challenge for both targeted therapies and immunotherapies in cancer. Arginine starvation has proven a promising strategy to overcome recurrent tumors. However, key molecules involved and how immune responses are elicited are not well understood. Here we identify in melanoma cells MYC-ATF4-ASS1 signaling as a pathway, which not only governs intracellular arginine synthesis but also modulates antitumor immunity. ATF4 knockout in melanoma cells phenocopied ASS1 knockout in the same cells, both showing greater sensitivity to arginine depletors such as ADI-PEG20. A combination strategy of BRAF/MEK inhibitors and an arginine depletor shows significant therapeutic effects in a immune-compromised mouse model. Both Atf4 and Ass1 knockout melanomas exhibited enhanced infiltration of Cd8+ T cells and significantly reduced tumor growth in a syngeneic mouse model. Single cell transcriptomics profiled the reshaped tumor microenvironment and revealed that a subset of resident macrophages were reprogrammed by endogenous arginine blockade. Overall, our findings reveal that the MYC-ATF4-ASS1 axis not only controls arginine vulnerability of melanomas but also shapes the immune microenvironment.

title: NSCLC KRAS G12C MUTANT CELLS ARE DEPENDENT ON MUC1-C FOR RESISTANCE TO KRAS INHIBITORS [MGH1112]
summary: Treatment of NSCLC KRAS G12C mutant tumors with targeted KRAS inhibitors, such as sotorasib and adagrasib, is invariably associated with the emergence of acquired resistance. The mechanisms responsible for resistance to these agents have largely remained unclear. We report that patients with NSCLC KRAS G12C tumors expressing increased levels of the MUC1 gene exhibit decreases in overall survival in response to sotorasib and adagrasib. In investigating the basis for this finding, we found that exposure of NSCLC KRAS G12C mutant cells to these agents induces expression of the oncogenic MUC1-C/M1C protein. We show that M1C induction is STAT1 dependent and that targeting M1C increases sensitivity to sotorasib. Studies of sotorasib-resistant (SR) cells further reveal upregulation of M1C chromatin levels in association with activation of the epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT). Mechanistically, M1C drives NF-kB p65-mediated induction of the ZEB1 EMT-TF. Furthermore, targeting M1C NF-kB ZEB1 signaling suppresses EMT and sotorasib resistance. Having identified this M1C dependence, we demonstrate that targeting M1C with an antibody-drug conjugate (ADC) is effective against sotorasib-resistant cells growing in vitro and as tumor xenografts. These findings identify M1C as a major effector of sotorasib resistance and as a target for ADC treatment of patients with refractory NSCLC KRAS G12C mutant tumors.

title: PITX1 Safeguards Epithelial Identity and Constrains EMT via Transcriptional and Epigenetic Control
summary: Epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) drives tumor progression, metastasis, and therapeutic resistance, yet the upstream mechanisms that safeguard epithelial identity are incompletely understood. Here, we identify the homeobox transcription factor PITX1 as a central regulator of epithelial identity and a suppressor of EMT. Integrative chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq), transcriptional profiling (RNA-seq), and CUT&RUN analyses in TGFβ-induced EMT models reveal that PITX1 selectively occupies promoters of epithelial-specific genes in the epithelial state and is downregulated during EMT progression. Loss of PITX1 is sufficient to activate mesenchymal gene expression, induce cytoskeletal remodelling, and drive nuclear morphological changes consistent with EMT, even in the absence of exogenous stimuli, demonstrating that PITX1 constrains epithelial plasticity at both chromatin and transcriptional levels. In breast tumors, PITX1 is enriched in epithelial tumor compartments and EMT-low subtypes but repressed in EMT-high, mesenchymal-like cancers. Notably, PITX1 is well-known for its roles in hindlimb and pituitary patterning, suggesting that developmental transcription factors are repurposed to maintain epithelial stability in adult tissues. Together, our findings position PITX1 as a transcriptional and epigenetic safeguard of epithelial identity whose repression serves as a molecular gateway for EMT and tumor plasticity, with implications for therapeutic strategies aimed at reinforcing epithelial differentiation.

title: Somatic TP53 Mutations Drive T and NK Cell Dysfunction and Create an Inflammatory Immune Niche in Acute Myeloid Leukemia
summary: TP53-mutant acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is characterized by poor prognosis and limited response to immunotherapy, yet the mechanisms underlying immune failure in this setting remain unclear. Here, we integrate single-cell DNA sequencing with surface proteomics to demonstrate that somatic TP53 mutations arise not only in leukemic blasts but also in T and NK cells from patients with TP53-mutant AML. TP53-mutant T cells exhibit enhanced exhaustion phenotypes, impaired cytotoxic function, and altered clonal architecture. Mechanistically, mutant p53 reprograms T cells toward a pro-inflammatory yet dysfunctional state, reshaping cytokine networks and promoting a niche enriched in inflammatory and myeloid-supportive signals. These mutant T cells impair both intrinsic effector function and the functionality of surrounding immune cells. Introduction of TP53 mutations into healthy donor T cells recapitulates exhaustion and impaired tumor control, whereas elimination of mutant p53 restores effector function, normalizes cytokine programs, and improves disease control in a TP53-mutant AML xenograft model.

title: Transcription Factor Subtype Governs Response and Resistance to DLL3-Directed T-Cell Engagement in Small Cell Lung Cancer [scRNA-seq]
summary: Although small cell lung cancer (SCLC) comprises transcription factor (TF)-defined molecular subtypes (ASCL1, NEUROD1, POU2F3), the extent to which these subtypes predict response to effective therapy—and whether therapy can select for subtype switching—remains unknown. The recent approval of the DLL3×CD3 bispecific T-cell engager tarlatamab represents one of the first meaningful advances in relapsed small cell lung cancer (SCLC) in decades, yet responses remain heterogeneous and resistance is inevitable. Here, we profiled cell-free circulating chromatin from prospectively collected patient plasma (46 patients; 167 samples) and applied APEX to infer tumor gene expression at single-gene resolution, enabling interrogation of response and acquired resistance to tarlatamab. Parallel development of the first immunocompetent syngeneic mouse model to study tarlatamab response and resistance enabled functional validation. Across species, findings converged on a central principle: TF subtype governs both initial response and acquired resistance. Therapeutic response was significantly associated with ASCL1⁺ tumors, whereas NEUROD1⁺ tumors exhibited inferior responses and POU2F3⁺ tumors were uniformly resistant, consistent with DLL3 being a direct ASCL1 transcriptional target and most highly expressed in ASCL1⁺ tumors. Strikingly, one mode of acquired resistance converged on therapeutic selection for a NEUROD1-high state with concomitant DLL3 downregulation. Some tumors also exhibited enrichment of regulatory and exhausted T-cell programs underscoring tarlatamab’s dual-targeting mechanism of action. Together, these results reveal that under tarlatamab pressure, tumors select against ASCL1-driven cell states, driving resistance to an antigen intrinsically linked to ASCL1 activity. These findings establish the clinical relevance of TF-defined molecular subtypes in human SCLC. More broadly, they highlight the power of integrating longitudinal in vivo plasma transcriptional profiling in patients with functional mouse modeling to uncover clinical and biological mechanisms of response and resistance to cell-surface-targeted therapies.

title: Altretamine induces ferroptosis in small cell lung cancer by promoting epigenetic silencing and lysosomal degradation of GPX4
summary: Background: Small cell lung cancer (SCLC) is a high-grade and aggressive neuroendocrine carcinoma that remains incurable due to the emergence of drug resistance and frequent relapse. This study aimed to clarify the therapeutic potential and detailed mechanism of altretamine against SCLC.Methods: Altretamine-triggered cytotoxicity and lipid peroxidation were determined by EdU, FerroOrange probes, etc. GPX4 promoter methylation was evaluated by Methylation-specific PCR, chromatin immunoprecipitation, etc. Altretamine-induced GPX4 degradation was examined by bio-layer interferometry, immunoprecipitation, etc. Results: Altretamine mainly initiates ferroptosis in SCLC cells, accompanied by accumulation of intracellular ROS and lipid peroxidation. Mechanistically, altretamine facilitated the binding of DNMT3A to GPX4 promoter, leading to DNA methylation of GPX4 gene and subsequent transcriptional repression. Moreover, altretamine directly bound to GPX4 protein and accelerated the lysosomal degradation of GPX4 protein in a HSC70-dependent manner. Inhibition of DNA demethylation by inactivating Ten-eleven translocation (TET) proteins synergistically strengthened the anti-SCLC activity of altretamine.Conclusions: Our findings revealed the first time that altretamine induced ferroptotic cell death by promoting DNMT3A-mediated epigenetic silencing of GPX4 gene and HSC70-mediated lysosomal degradation of GPX4 protein in SCLC cells. Altretamine alone or in combination with TET inhibitors is a valuable and credible strategy for the clinical treatment of SCLC.

title: LEDGF/p75 mediates chemoresistance in leukemia in a context dependent manner
summary: The study focused on characterization of the role of LEDGF/p75 in chemoresistance of different leukemic subtypes.Abstract:Lens epithelium-derived growth factor p75 (LEDGF/p75), also known as PSIP1, is a chromatin associated protein that interacts with multiple partners, including HIV integrase and KMT2A. In KMT2A-rearranged leukemia (KMT2A-r), LEDGF/p75 tethers KMT2A fusion complex to chromatin and is essential for leukemogenesis. Beyond KMT2A-r leukemia, LEDGF/p75 has emerged as an oncogenic factor associated with cancer cell survival and resistance to therapy. However, its role in drug resistance across different leukemic subtypes remains poorly defined. Here, we investigated the contribution of LEDGF/p75 to therapy resistance in multiple leukemia models with distinct genetic backgrounds. We show that LEDGF/p75 depletion sensitizes KMT2A-r T-ALL cells to cytarabine. In contrast, LEDGF/p75 depletion in KMT2A-r B-ALL cells protected against cytarabine induced cell death, highlighting a context dependent role of LEDGF/p75. Notably, in chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) cells harboring BCR-ABL fusion, loss of LEDGF/p75 increased sensitivity to the chemotherapy vincristine as well as to BCR-ABL inhibitors. Mechanistically, transcriptomic and protein analysis revealed that LEDGF/p75 depletion reduced JAK-STAT signaling, with decreased level of activated JAK2 and STAT5. This was accompanied by enrichment of stress and apoptotic transcriptional programs, suppression of proliferation and DNA replication/repair pathways and reduced drug resistance gene signatures. Together, these findings demonstrate a context dependent role of LEDGF/p75 in leukemic therapy resistance and identify LEDGF/p75 as potential therapeutic vulnerability that could be exploited to enhance treatment sensitivity in selected leukemic subtypes, including BCR-ABL positive CML.

title: Cell-free RNA Signatures Derived from the Tumor Microenvironment Predict Outcomes of CAR-T Therapy in Large B Cell Lymphoma
summary: Anti-CD19 chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy can induce durable remissions in patients with large B-cell lymphoma (LBCL), yet outcomes remain variable. title: CDK2/9 Blockade Remodels Chromatin and Drives Phenotypic Plasticity in glioblastoma organoids
summary: Glioblastoma (GBM) remains a highly lethal brain tumor with limited therapeutic options and widespread resistance to standard treatments. Cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs), key regulators of cell cycle progression and transcription, are frequently dysregulated in GBM, contributing to tumor pathogenesis. title: Endogenous PD-L1-Blocking Antibodies Drive Potent Anti-Tumor Immunity
summary: Checkpoint blockade therapy, though transformative, remains ineffective in 70-80% of patients, with autoimmune adverse effects. title: Aberrant stabilization of the m6A reader IGF2BP3 drives metastatic progression and 5-FU refractoriness in FBXW7-mutant colorectal cancer
summary: FBXW7 is mutated in approximately 10% of colorectal cancers (CRC), and the vast majority of these alterations are loss-of-function mutations that abrogate its E3 ligase activity. title: CASP10-mediated suppression of GSDME-dependent pyroptosis shapes the tumor immune microenvironment in hepatocellular carcinoma
summary: Cancer cells evade immune surveillance by suppressing inflammatory cell death, yet the underlying molecular mechanisms remain incompletely understood. Whether alternative caspase-mediated cleavage of GSDME can suppress pyroptosis has not been explored. Caspase-10 (CASP10) is an initiator caspase that is absent in mice and rats and shares high sequence homology with CASP8. Its substrate specificity and role in cancer cell death remain poorly defined. Here we show that in liver cancer, CASP10 cleaves GSDME at an alternative site (D16), generating a short GSDME-N fragment (amino acids 17–270) that lacks pyroptosis activity. Loss of the N-terminal 1–16 amino acids eliminates the α1 thumb structure required for membrane insertion, abrogating both plasma membrane binding and mitochondrial targeting. Furthermore, short GSDME-N associates with canonical GSDME-N and blocks its oligomerization, thereby suppressing pyroptosis. In vivo experiments and single-cell transcriptomic analysis of human liver cancer demonstrate that CASP10 promotes immune evasion and is associated with invasive metastatic progression. Targeting CASP10 with antisense oligonucleotides restores pyroptosis and suppresses tumor growth. These findings reveal CASP10-mediated alternative cleavage of GSDME as a pyroptosis-suppressive mechanism in cancer, and identify CASP10 as a therapeutic target and a biomarker of metastatic progression in liver cancer.

title: Structural Basis of Cooperative COMPASS Activation by Histone Acetylation and Ubiquitination [RNA-seq]
summary: Histone modifications encode regulatory information that shapes chromatin architecture and transcriptional programs. Among them, histone acetylation is a paradigm for gene regulation, yet how it directly modulates chromatin-modifying enzymes remains unresolved. The COMPASS/MLL complex, a key methyltransferase that catalyzes H3K4 methylation, integrates multiple histone marks to fine-tune transcription. While H2B ubiquitination (H2BUb) is a well- established COMPASS activator, the mechanism of histone acetylation in regulating its enzymatic activity has remained unclear. Here, we reveal that H3 lysine 14 acetylation (H3K14ac) directly enhances COMPASS activity by increasing substrate accessibility and stabilizing nucleosome engagement, acting cooperatively with H2BUb to promote efficient H3K4 methylation. Cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) shows that H3K14ac directly reinforces COMPASS stabilization on nucleosomes through interactions with a highly conserved surface of the Bre2 subunit, facilitating catalysis. Biochemical assays demonstrate that H3K14ac amplifies COMPASS activity in a Bre2-dependent manner, with H2BUb further reinforcing this activation and facilitating trimethylation of H3K4. Notably, disruption of Bre2-H3K14ac recognition abolishes this effect, revealing a hierarchical mechanism in which H3 acetylation primes COMPASS for activation, while H2B ubiquitination locks the complex into a catalytically competent state. Functionally, H3K14ac is required for proper RNA polymerase II elongation, and its loss represses key genes such as Hoxa9 and Hoxa10, which are essential for leukemic stem cell maintenance in AML. These findings extend the role of histone acetylation beyond chromatin accessibility to active chromatin signaling, redefining how histone modifications integrate chromatin state and enzymatic function, with broad implications for transcriptional regulation and epigenetic therapy.

title: Colorectal cancer heterogeneity co-evolves with tumor architecture to determine disease outcome [scRNA-seq]
summary: Intratumoral heterogeneity, originating from genetic, epigenetic, and phenotypic cellular diversity, is pervasive in cancer. As these heterogeneous states employ diverse mechanisms to promote tumor progression, metastasis, and therapy resistance, emergence of cancer heterogeneity is one of the most significant barriers to curative treatment. Here we leverage deep learning approaches to develop a high-throughput image-analysis paradigm with subcellular resolution that quantifies and predicts colorectal cancer (CRC) patient outcome based on tissue architecture and nuclear morphology. We further combine this approach with spatial transcriptomics, multiplex immunohistochemistry, and patient-derived organoids to uncover a dynamic, co-evolutionary relationship between tumor architecture and cell states. We identify clinically relevant architectural interfaces in CRC tissue that diversify cellular identities by favoring distinct cancer stem cell states and thus promote evolution of tumor heterogeneity. Specifically, tissue fragmentation and associated compressive forces through YAP activity promote loss of classic stem cell signature and acquisition of fetal/regenerative stem cell states, which initially emerges as a hybrid state with features of epithelial-to-mesenchyme (EMT) transition. Additional tumor stroma communication then diversifies these states into distinct stem cell and EMT states at the invasive margins of tumors. Reciprocally, beta-catenin activity state of tumor cells tunes their responsiveness to tissue architecture. Collectively, this work uncovers a feedback loop between cell states and tissue architecture that drives cancer heterogeneity and cell state diversification. Machine learning-based analyses harness this co-dependency, independently of mutational status or cancer stage, to predict patient outcome.

title: B7-H3 mediates immune escape and metastasis in SCLC through CXCL11/CXCR7/NFIB axis
summary: Small-cell lung cancer (SCLC) is an aggressive malignancy that is generally considered an immune desert. title: Development and preclinical evaluation of a decoy DLL4-encoding oncolytic HSV-1 for solid tumors
summary: Preclinical and clinical investigation of oncolytic HSV-1 (oHSV) treatment for cancer has indicated increased Notch signaling in tumors after treatment. Since Notch activation often heralds cancer cell stemness, angiogenesis, and invasion, the induction of this pathway after oHSV virotherapy can support tumor growth and limit response to virotherapy. Here, we evaluated the impact of blocking DLL4, a Notch ligand, on virotherapy. Matched tumor biopsies pre- and post-oHSV (CAN-3110, NCT03152318) treatment revealed an induction of DLL4 post-therapy. We observed that expression of a recombinant soluble decoy DLL4 (sDLL4) could block Notch activation in tumor cells. Thus, we engineered an oHSV vector designed to encode for soluble DLL4 (OVsDLL4) to block DLL4-mediated signaling. RNA sequencing and gene set enrichment analysis revealed that, relative to control oHSV, OVsDLL4 blocked Notch and sprouting angiogenesis pathways after treatment. Despite slower virus replication in vitro, OVsDLL4 cytotoxicity remained effective against tumor cells. Transcriptome profiling also indicated a significant dysregulation of metabolic pathways related to oxidative phosphorylation and glutathione metabolism, in accordance with increased oxygen consumption observed by Seahorse analysis in cells expressing sDLL4. OVsDLL4-treated cells further showed increased reactive oxygen species relative to control oHSV-treated cells. Co-culture of infected tumor cells with macrophages revealed that OVsDLL4 treatment educated macrophage gene expression towards an inflammatory polarization. In vivo, the therapeutic efficacy of OVsDLL4 was underscored after treatment of mice bearing different solid tumors resulted in reduced tumor burden and prolonged survival.

title: Trogocytosis of cancer-associated fibroblasts promotes pancreatic cancer growth and immune suppression via phospholipid scramblase anoctamin 6 (ANO6).
summary: In pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), the fibroblastic stroma constitutes most of the tumour mass and is remarkably devoid of functional blood vessels. We have also determined that CAF-expressed phospholipid scramblase anoctamin 6 (ANO6) is an essential regulator of CAF trogocytosis required to promote PDAC cell survival. This influx activates ANO6 and results in phosphatidylserine exposure on CAF plasma membranes, initiating trogocytosis and transfer of membrane lipids, including cholesterol, to PDAC cells. Importantly, ANO6-dependent phosphatidylserine externalization supports the immunosuppressive function of pancreatic CAFs towards cytotoxic T cells by promoting trogocytosis of the CAF plasma membrane. Furthermore, blockade of ANO6 antagonizes tumour growth by disrupting delivery of exogenous cholesterol to cancer cells and reverses immune suppression, suggesting a potential new strategy for PDAC therapy.

summary: Chemotherapy remains the backbone of neoadjuvant treatment for triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC), and response to chemotherapy strongly correlates with patient prognosis. title: Clusterin Expression Helps Distinguish Idiopathic Multicentric Castleman Disease from Select Lymphadenopathies
summary: Idiopathic multicentric Castleman disease (iMCD) is a heterogeneous cytokine storm disorder involving systemic inflammation, multicentric lymphadenopathy with characteristic histopathology, and life-threatening multiple organ dysfunction. Patients can present with symptoms ranging from thrombocytopenia, anasarca, fever/elevated C-reactive protein (CRP), reticulin myelofibrosis, renal dysfunction, and organomegaly (iMCD-TAFRO) to thrombocytosis, hypergammaglobulinemia, and plasmacytosis (iMCD-IPL), with patients not falling into either group (iMCD-NOS). The molecular mechanisms across the clinical subtypes have not been elucidated and new effective treatments are needed. Here, we performed bulk RNA sequencing and targeted gene expression quantification in lymph node tissue from multiple iMCD clinical subtypes, pathologically related disorders, and controls. We identified 249 upregulated and 42 downregulated genes in iMCD-TAFRO lymph node tissue, which were enriched in the following pathways: angiogenesis, cell proliferation, and various aspects of the humoral and innate immune response. The targeted gene expression analysis revealed shared differentially expressed genes (DEGs) across all three iMCD clinical subtypes, including SPP1, XBP1, PRDM1, and CLU. We identified unique DEGs in each iMCD clinical subtype, including PLA2G2A, MSR1, IL8 (iMCD-TAFRO), IL9, KIR3DL1, IL18RAP (iMCD-IPL), and IL7, TLR8, and CX3CR1 (iMCD-NOS). Since Clusterin (CLU) was significantly upregulated in iMCD but not in related conditions, we performed immunohistochemistry and observed that Clusterin is elevated in the germinal center and mantle zone regions of iMCD patient lymph nodes. Together, this work identified pathways dysregulated in iMCD lymph nodes and suggests that Clusterin could be a novel biomarker.

title: Ultrasound-Mediated BBB Opening Promotes Microglial Reprogramming and Enhanced Endothelial Interactions in the Human Peritumoral Brain [Multiome_scATAC_RNAseq]
summary: The blood–brain barrier (BBB) restricts entry of therapeutics and shapes immune surveillance in the central nervous system, while microglia maintain barrier integrity and coordinate repair. Low-intensity pulsed ultrasound with intravenously administered microbubbles (LIPU/MB) transiently opens the BBB in patients, with restoration mostly occurring within about an hour; however, how microglia respond to LIPU/MB during this acute repair window in the human brain remains unknown. We report on intraoperative LIPU/MB studies where the peritumoral brain of glioblastoma patients was biopsied 45 minutes after sonication and analyzed, as part of phase I/II clinical trials (NCT04528680). We integrated single-cell RNA-seq, single-cell ATAC-seq, spatial transcriptomics, and multiplex immunofluorescence. We observe that LIPU/MB modulates perivascular microglia by promoting extension of processes toward the endothelium, inducing pro-inflammatory and chemoattractant transcriptional programs, and remodeling of endothelial–myeloid ligand–receptor communication. We find that microglial reprogramming is accompanied by coordinated changes in chromatin accessibility and heightened activity of the AP-1 transcription factor complex. These results reveal that LIPU/MB-based BBB opening in humans does not merely permit drug passage but reprograms resident myeloid cells to engage the vasculature and amplify innate and adaptive immune pathways, providing a mechanistic basis to leverage immune activation by LIPU/MB with immunotherapies for brain tumors. These findings also warrant consideration in the context of the pathophysiology and therapeutics of CNS diseases where there is acute BBB disruption, or where LIPU/MB is under investigation.

title: Modeling the active proteome by context-matched perturbation signatures
summary: Measuring protein activity on a global scale remains a central challenge in molecular biology. We hypothesized that the functional contribution of proteins to cellular processes can be inferred from perturbation-induced transcriptomic changes using context-matched reference signatures. Here we present, a computational framework that estimates thousands of protein activities (currently ~4800) from gene expression at scale, by leveraging context-specific references across major cancer types. In benchmarking analyses, VMPA achieved robust predictive performance (precision-recall AUC > 0.88), inferring activity estimates across diverse protein classes, including kinases, metabolic enzymes, receptors, and transcription factors. Applied to glioblastoma, VMPA tracked protein activity following targeted inhibitor treatments, enabling inference of drug effects on specific protein targets. Furthermore, VMPA identified nine recurrent malignant glioblastoma cell states based on the activity of 2,700 proteins, exposing subpopulations not detectable with gene expression data alone. Finally, we demonstrate the use of VMPA in discovery-driven research by uncovering previously unknown cancer-driver activities in experimental models. In summary, VMPA maps the "active proteome", the ensemble of proteins in their functional states, by inferring protein activity from transcriptomic data, providing a versatile tool for exploring protein function at scale in complex biological systems.

title: Integrative discovery and functional dependency mapping uncover essential chimeric RNAs in the active transcriptome
summary: Chimeric RNAs are a class of molecules defined as RNA transcripts containing genetic information for multiple genes. While their expression patterns across tissue types and disease states have been well-documented, the biological function of these transcripts remains poorly understood. In this study, we developed an integrative prediction pipeline to establish an atlas of 569,640 chimeric RNAs across 1,019 cancer cell lines. Leveraging this resource, we performed a systematic functional dependency screen by integrating our predictions with perturbation datasets from The Cancer Dependency Map project. This approach moves beyond prediction to identifying high-confidence functional chimeric RNAs essential for cellular processes, including a subset of recurrent chimeric transcripts generated by cis-splicing of adjacent genes. We demonstrate that depletion of selected candidate chimeras disrupts cell cycle progression and cellular fitness and that these transcripts are frequently dysregulated in primary breast tumors. Together, these results demonstrate that chimeric RNAs constitute a previously underappreciated layer of gene expression, expanding the functional genome beyond conventional genetics.

summary: Metastatic progression depends on the systemic remodeling of distant host tissues before tumor cell arrival, yet the tumor-derived signals that orchestrate this process remain poorly understood. Mechanistically, this response was driven by LO-associated nucleic acids activating convergent cytosolic DNA- and RNA-sensing pathways in recipient stromal cells. LO-conditioned BM-MSCs promoted the accumulation and polarization of neutrophils toward an immunosuppressive, polymorphonuclear myeloid-derived suppressor cell (PMN-MDSC) phenotype. In vivo, genetic suppression of LO shedding in tumor cells reduced PMN-MDSC accumulation in the bone marrow, and this was rescued by systemic LO administration. Together, these findings establish LOs as specialized carriers of immunomodulatory signals that reprogram the bone marrow microenvironment to support metastatic colonization, identifying a previously unrecognized mechanism linking tumor vesiculation to early immune remodeling at distant sites.

summary: T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL) remains incurable for many patients who relapse, largely because conventional chemotherapy fails to eradicate leukemia stem cells (LSCs). title: Targeting mutant p53 aggregates in pancreatic cancer using an autophagy-targeting chimera
summary: Protein aggregation is increasingly recognized as a fundamental feature of cancer biology, particularly in tumors experiencing chronic proteotoxic stress. TP53 is the most frequent mutated gene in human cancers, and many cancer-associated missense mutations promote protein misfolding and amyloid-like aggregation. These aggregates abrogate wild-type tumor-suppressive functions while conferring oncogenic gain-of-function (GOF) activities that drive tumor progression and resistance to therapy. Despite decades of effort, direct pharmacologic targeting of mutant p53 has remained challenging due to the absence of a druggable pocket and the extensive mutational heterogeneity of p53. Here, we employed the AUTOTAC platform to target mutant p53 aggregates by exploiting aggregation-associated conformational features characteristic of β-sheet-rich oligomers and protofibrillar aggregates. ATC-37 was designed to link a methylene blue-derived amyloid-binding ligand, which preferentially recognizes β-sheet-rich protein aggregates, to an autophagy-targeting ligand (ATL) that allosterically activates the autophagy receptor p62/SQSTM1. This design enables engagement of amyloid-like mutant p53 aggregates and promotes their recruitment to autophagosomes. ATC-37 displays a dual, dose-dependent mechanism of action. At low concentrations, it promotes autophagic degradation of mutant p53 aggregates and suppresses downstream GOF signaling. At higher concentrations, it induces robust p62-dependent sequestration of mutant p53 aggregates that exceeds autophagic capacity, triggering proteotoxic cell death. In a pancreatic cancer xenograft model using PANC-1 cells, ATC-37 significantly inhibited tumor growth, reduced amyloid-like mutant p53 aggregates, and suppressed angiogenesis. Importantly, ATC-37 synergized with radiotherapy, overcoming mutant p53-associated radioresistance. These findings establish aggregation-state-directed AUTOTAC therapy as a conceptually innovative and mutation-agonistic strategy for targeting mutant p53 and other aggregation-prone oncoproteins.

Therefore, persister cells can be efficiently eliminated by sequentially treating with ferroptosis and cuproptosis inducers.

title: Expression profiles of lncRNAs and mRNAs in AGS cells treated with O-prenylchalcone 7e
summary: This study aimed to characterize the changes in lncRNA and mRNA expression profiles induced by O-prenylchalcone 7e in AGS gastric cancer cells. Background: Gastric cancer remains one of the leading causes of cancer-related mortality worldwide, highlighting the need to identify novel therapeutic strategies targeting the molecular networks involved in tumor progression. Although new therapeutic compounds show promising properties, the antitumor mechanisms activated by noncoding RNAs (ncRNAs) remain largely unexplored. In this study, we evaluated the effects of the novel compound O-prenylchalcone 7e on proliferation and cell death, with a particular focus on the transcriptome reprogramming mediated by long noncoding RNAs (lncRNAs) and messenger RNAs (mRNAs) networks in gastric cancer cells. Methods: AGS cells were treated with O-prenylchalcone 7e and subjected to transcriptomic analysis of mRNAs and lncRNAs using Clariom™ D Human microarrays. Differentially expressed transcripts were analyzed by functional enrichment using GO, KEGG, and GSEA tools. LncRNA–miRNA–mRNA networks were constructed through co-expression analysis using Cytoscape. Candidate lncRNAs and mRNA expression were validated by RT-qPCR assays. LncRNA OVCH1-AS1 silencing was achieved by transfection of specific siRNAs. MiR-181a-5p ectopic overexpression was performed by transfection of the miRNA precursor. OVCH1-AS1 silencing and miR-181a-5p overexpression were assessed by RT-qPCR assays. RHOB protein levels were determined by Western blot. Cell proliferation was evaluated using MTT assays. Apoptosis analysis was performed via Annexin V/7-AAD staining and flow cytometry. Mitochondrial membrane potential was analyzed using the MitoOrange dye and flow cytometry. Results: Our data showed that O-prenylchalcone 7e reprogrammed the lncRNAs and mRNA transcriptome of AGS gastric cancer cells. Expression profiling using microarrays identified 261 differentially expressed lncRNAs, of which 146 were upregulated and 115 were downregulated following 48 h treatment with O-prenylchalcone 7e (IC50 49.15 μM). Moreover, 221 mRNAs were differentially expressed, including 56 upregulated and 165 downregulated transcripts. Enrichment and correlation analyses revealed that the upregulated lncRNAs, including OVCH1-AS1, NORAD, MIR4435-2HG, DKK4-1, and PAQR9-2, as well as the overexpressed mRNAs RHOB, BCL10, DDIT3, CSNK2A3, and FZD5, among others, were associated with processes related to apoptosis and cancer-related signaling pathways. Interestingly, we identified a novel OVCH1-AS1/miR-181a-5p/RHOB axis as a potential module regulated by O-prenylchalcone 7e. RT-qPCR assays confirmed the modulation of the OVCH1-AS1/miR-181a-5p/RHOB axis in AGS and NCI-N87 gastric cancer cells. Interestingly, OVCH1-AS1 silencing increased miR-181a-5p levels, whereas miR-181a-5p overexpression significantly reduced RHOB at mRNA and protein levels. Western blot experiments confirmed that O-prenylchalcone 7e increased RHOB protein, whereas OVCH1-AS1 silencing or miR-181a-5p overexpression also reduced RHOB levels. Remarkably, silencing of OVCH1-AS1 and overexpression of miR-181a-5p partially reversed the antiproliferative effects induced by O-prenylchalcone 7e in AGS and NCI-N87 cancer cells. Furthermore, both strategies reduced the compound-induced cell death, decreasing the apoptotic population. Finally, OVCH1-AS1-deficient cells and miR-181a-5p-overexpressing cancer cells showed a significant attenuation of the depolarization of the mitochondrial membrane in response to drug treatment. Conclusions: Our data suggest that O-prenylchalcone 7e induces a transcriptional remodeling in gastric cancer cells, involving the regulation of lncRNA/mRNA-mediated regulatory networks. The identification of the OVCH1-AS1/miR-181a-5p/RHOB axis reveals a potential ncRNA-dependent mechanism associated with the anticancer response induced by the drug. These findings expand our understanding of the role of lncRNAs in the molecular mechanisms underlying bioactive compounds and ultimately suggest a therapeutic potential of O-prenylchalcone 7e as a candidate drug for the development of novel strategies against gastric cancer.

title: Preclinical Evaluation of Ixazomib for High-Risk Pediatric Brain Tumors
summary: Many of the highest-risk pediatric brain cancers continue to experience poor clinical outcomes despite intensification of current multimodal therapies. Proteasome inhibition has shown preclinical promise across a range of cancer models, including diffuse midline glioma (DMG), medulloblastoma, and atypical teratoid/rhabdoid tumors (ATRT), although clinically viable agents have been limited. Recent studies in adults with glioblastoma suggest that ixazomib, a second-generation proteasome inhibitor, may achieve therapeutic concentrations in the central nervous system (CNS), raising the possibility that a CNS-penetrant proteasome inhibitor could similarly provide therapeutic benefit in childhood brain cancers. Here, ixazomib was evaluated in cell lines and orthotopic xenograft models of DMG, MYC-amplified medulloblastoma (MYC-MB), and ATRT. RNA sequencing and LC-MS-based proteomics were used to define the functional consequences of ixazomib treatment, while proteasome activity measurements were used to assess ixazomib activity across the blood-brain barrier. Ixazomib demonstrated consistent cytotoxic effects across high-risk pediatric brain tumor models at low nanomolar concentrations and induced proteostatic stress responses and apoptosis. However, ixazomib treatment did not confer a survival benefit in orthotopic models, and pharmacodynamic testing indicated insufficient inhibition of proteasome activity within the CNS compared with extracranial tissues. These findings demonstrate that although multiple pediatric brain tumor models are susceptible to proteasome inhibition, ixazomib may lack sufficient blood-brain barrier penetration to serve as a translationally viable strategy for exploiting this therapeutic vulnerability.

title: Targeting Distinct Cell Cycle Nodes Overcomes KRAS/RAS Inhibitor Resistance
summary: Activating mutations in KRAS drive pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) and non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Although mutant-selective KRAS inhibitors and pan-RAS inhibitors provide clinical benefits, the development of resistance limits durable response. Transcriptomic and proteomic analyses reveal that, despite effective suppression of mutant KRAS signaling, resistant cells sustain cell cycle progression. Distinct orthogonal mitogenic pathways are engaged in a context-dependent manner to bypass KRAS inhibition. While these pathways can be broadly inhibited using the pan-RAS-ON inhibitor RMC-6236, cells remained capable of developing acquired resistance where cell proliferation is uncoupled from RAS signaling. Combinatorial drug screens and genome-wide CRISPR-Cas9 screens reveal that perturbing cell cycle nodes via targeting cyclin dependent kinases CDK4/6 and CDK2 could restore sensitivity to KRAS/RAS inhibitors. Co-targeting CDK4/6 induces G1 arrest and suppresses E2F-regulated proteins across all resistant models. In contrast, co-targeting CDK2 exerts a broader effect by impairing DNA replication, inducing G2 arrest, preventing mitotic entry, and yielding a more durable cytostatic response that delays cellular outgrowth after drug withdrawal. Finally, concurrent inhibition of KRAS with either CDK4/6 or CDK2 yields durable tumor control in vivo in xenografts derived from acquired resistant models. In conclusion, our findings identify sustained cell cycle activity as a defining feature of resistance to KRAS-directed therapies and establish cell cycle co-targeting as an effective strategy to overcome KRAS/RAS inhibitor resistance.

title: Multi-omics and spatial analysis of microgravity-grown glioblastoma organoids reveals superior modeling of advanced disease after long-term spaceflight
summary: Creating accurate organoid models remains a challenge, particularly for diseases like glioblastoma (GBM), an aggressive, treatment-resistant brain cancer with an immunosuppressive microenvironment. To overcome limitations of Earth-based models (sedimentation and disaggregation) and leverage the unique advantages of space (accelerated disease progression and immune dysregulation), this study utilizes a panel of GBM-myeloid organoids cultured for 40 days aboard the International Space Station. Spaceflight-grown GBM organoids have more uniform morphology compared to ground controls. We observed a context-dependent response to spaceflight, with the inclusion of macrophages and monocytes altering the bulk and spatial transcriptional response. While GBM-alone organoids have transcriptional markers of less aggressive disease in microgravity, organoids containing GBM cells + monocytes have increased expression of genes associated with disease progression and poor patient outcomes. Gene expression patterns are more spatially organized, with mesenchymal-related genes enriched in the core and inflammation-related genes enriched at the periphery, mimicking GBM tumor architecture. Microgravity-grown GBM+monocyte organoids exhibit increased secretion of proteins such as CXCL12 and LOX-1, associated with more aggressive disease. Infrared chemical imaging confirms spatial chemical gradients of DNA, protein, and lipid species in both space- and terrestrially-grown organoids. In summary, this work presents not only a novel, advanced model of glioblastoma for basic and translational research but also demonstrates methods to acquire diverse data from organoids compatible with the unique constraints of in-space systems, helping establish a working model for orbital oncology.

title: Gene transcription and chromatin packing domains form a self-organizing system [EU-Seq]
summary: The human genome organizes into several thousand chromatin packing domains that couple euchromatin and heterochromatin into unified nanoscale volumes. Prior work suggested these domains form by transcriptionally driven loops that guide packing domain assembly. Here, we study the process of transcriptionally driven domain formation and maintenance. By pairing auxin-inducible degron technology with nanoscopic imaging, transcriptomics, and Hi-C, we show that Pol-II regulates conformationally defined interphase chromatin packing domains. Pol-II facilitates nascent domain generation and maintains mature domain integrity through the process of generating transcriptional loops. Mechanistically, Pol-II maintains the packing of intronic and intergenic chromatin within domains by transcribing exons within gene bodies. Consequently, polymerase loss disrupts genome connectivity, in situ packing domains, and gene expression, genome-wide. Our findings suggest chromatin packing domains and RNA synthesis are tightly coupled to optimize transcriptional responses in human cells.

title: Identification of senescence-associated drivers of tumour growth and progression using a novel microarray platform
summary: Senescence and the senescence associated secretory phenotype (SASP) are implicated in promoting early tumorigenesis. However, it has been difficult to identify the responsible factors due to the complexity of SASP. Here we used canonical SASP factors on our microenvironment microarray (MEMA) platform to systematically identify SASP-associated drivers of tumorigenesis in breast and lung cancer cells. We found multiple SASP factors enhanced the proliferation and overall cell numbers for both lung and breast cells grown on the MEMA, and that there was significant overlap in SASP-associated growth-promoting factors between the two different cell types. The growth promoting ability of several factors, including IL-6, TGF-β and EGF, were validated in in vitro assays. Interestingly, these factors were effective in driving growth and survival in cells that were altered (either immortalized or fully transformed) but not in normal cells and impacted breast cells differently depending on the age of the patient. RNAseq identified upregulation of wound-healing and stem-cell programs in SASP factor-treated cells. Many of these same SASP factors were present in conditioned media collected from senescent cells, which enhanced the growth of both lung and breast cancer cells, and inhibitors of the specific SASP factors partially reduced growth, suggesting that effective tumorigenesis driven by SASP is multifactorial, which requires alterations in the target cells to achieve maximal response.

title: RNA fine-tunes KAT5 activity to shape chromatin acetylation during active transcription [RNA-Seq]
summary: KAT5 is a prominent histone acetyltransferase that deposits acetylation on histone H4 to regulate transcription, genome stability, and cell fate decisions. Although the chromatin recruitment of KAT5 and its associated NuA4/TIP60 complex is well characterized, the molecular mechanisms that regulate its catalytic activity are still largely unknown. Here, we identify RNA as a direct and reversible modulator of KAT5 activity. Using single-end enhanced crosslinking and immunoprecipitation sequencing (seCLIP-seq), we find that KAT5 binds RNA in cells with a strong preference for GC-rich mRNA sequences enriched near transcription start sites. Unexpectedly, loss of KAT5–RNA interactions during acute transcriptional inhibition triggers rapid and pronounced promoter hyperacetylation in a KAT5-dependent manner. Biochemical and structural analyses reveal that RNA engages a regulatory RNA-binding region within the HAT domain, sterically blocking substrate access to the catalytic pocket and thereby suppressing KAT5 acetyltransferase activity. Our findings uncover nascent RNA as a reversible allosteric inhibitor of KAT5, revealing an RNA-directed feedback mechanism that modulates promoter acetylation and transcriptional output.

title: Transcriptomic Profiling of adherent (2D) and spheroid (3D) cultures of SW480 colorectal cancer cells
summary: Cellular behavior and phenotype are profoundly influenced by the culture microenvironment. Traditional two-dimensional (2D) adherent culture systems, while widely used, fail to recapitulate the complex architecture, cell-cell interactions, and cell-matrix contacts that characterize the native tissue environment. In contrast, three-dimensional (3D) culture systems more faithfully mimic in vivo conditions, better reflecting the spatial organization, nutrient and oxygen gradients, and signaling dynamics found within tumors. Notably, 3D spheroid culture has emerged as a valuable approach for enriching stem-like cell populations, which are thought to drive tumor initiation, progression, therapeutic resistance, and recurrence. Understanding the transcriptomic differences between cells cultured under 2D and 3D conditions is therefore critical for interpreting in vitro findings and identifying the molecular programs associated with the stem-like state. In this study, we cultured SW480 colorectal cancer cells under two distinct conditions: conventional 2D adherent culture and 3D matrigel-based spheroid culture. To systematically characterize the transcriptomic differences between these two culture systems, we performed RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) analysis on cells derived from both conditions. This comparative approach enabled us to identify differentially expressed genes and associated biological pathways, providing insight into how the 3D spheroid microenvironment reprograms the transcriptome and potentially enriches for stem-like cellular characteristics in SW480 cells.

title: MAPK signaling links BRD2 chromatin occupancy to PI3K/AKT inhibitor sensitivity [RNA-Seq]
summary: Bromodomain and extra-terminal (BET) proteins, BRD2, BRD3, BRD4, and BRDT, are acetyl-lysine readers that couple histone acetylation to transcriptional output by recruiting elongation and transcription factor complexes to chromatin. BET proteins are promising therapeutic targets, but the functions of individual family members remain incompletely understood. Here we identify BRD2 as a co-targetable vulnerability with PI3K/AKT inhibition in breast cancer. Pan-BET inhibition and BRD2 knockout each synergized with PI3K pathway inhibitors in breast cancer cell lines, patient-derived organoids, and in vivo. BRD2 knockout impaired proliferation of triple-negative breast cancer cells and transcriptionally upregulated key signaling and stress response pathways, including the DNA damage response. Mechanistically, BRD2 is phosphorylated at Serine 37 (Ser37) by the mitogen- and stress-activated kinases MSK and RSK, and Ser37 phosphorylation is required for BRD2 chromatin binding and reader function. Together, these findings identify BRD2 as a phosphorylation-dependent, co-targetable vulnerability in PI3K pathway-inhibited breast cancer.

title: CDH1 loss remodels gene expression and lineage identity in human mammary epithelial cells [scRNA-Seq]
summary: Invasive lobular carcinoma (ILC) is a common subtype of breast cancer, molecularly defined by genetic loss of CDH1, and subsequent loss of cell adhesion protein E-cadherin, in ~95% of ILC. Though CDH1 loss occurs early in ILC oncogenesis, it is unclear how this facilitates transformation. We modeled early CDH1 loss using “normal” human mammary epithelial cells (HMEC), i.e. finite lifespan cells reflecting early hyperplasia, and targeted E-cadherin signaling using antibodies versus causing genetic CDH1 loss using siRNA or CRISPR/Cas9-knockout. Transcriptome analysis across four HMEC models showed that the mode of E-cadherin targeting is critical for the subsequent phenotype. Antibody-mediated inhibition of cell-cell contacts induced gene signatures of epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT), consistent with the role of E-cadherin suppression during the EMT process. Conversely, genetic CDH1 loss – as in ILC oncogenesis – repressed EMT signatures, and instead remodeled gene expression toward a luminal epithelial phenotype. RNA-seq, single cell transcriptomics, flow cytometry, microscopy, and ATACseq analyses support that CDH1 loss induces lineage remodeling to a luminal state, which is mirrored in transcriptomic analysis of clinical ILC precursor lesions. By isolating luminal versus basal cells prior to CDH1 knockout, we found that CDH1 loss led to remodeling of lineage identity in both populations, converging on a new lineage homeostasis with a luminal progenitor-like phenotype. Consistent with the shift to a luminal progenitor phenotype, CDH1 loss enhanced proliferative capacity over the finite lifespan of the HMECs, highlighting a feature of early CDH1 loss that may contribute to clonal advantage during tumor initiation. title: A Syngeneic Murine Glioma Model Recapitulates Key Molecular, Immunologic, and Functional Features of Human Glioblastoma Enabling Therapeutic Development
summary: Glioblastoma (GBM) is the most common and deadly primary brain tumor in adults, characterized by diffuse infiltrative lesions, distinct oncogenic alterations, and a suppressive tumor immune microenvironment (TIME). These traits, however, are not fully recapitulated in current syngeneic murine glioma models, thereby limiting the pre-clinical development of effective therapies. Here, we developed murine GBM models with patient-specific mutations that shared striking resemblance with human disease. Mosaic analysis with dual-recombinase mediated cassette exchange (MADR) and CRISPR-Cas9 were leveraged to generate autochthonous tumor models with single-copy somatic transgenesis of murine epidermal growth factor receptor variant III (mEGFRvIII) and loss-of-function mutations commonly observed in GBM. Characterization of a model lacking Pten and Cdkn2a (mEGFRvIII-PC) via histopathologic analyses, functional assays, and single-cell RNA sequencing showed these tumors developed as diffuse, infiltrative lesions with ill-defined margins and a necrotic core. The TIME was primarily comprised of microglia with minimal lymphocyte infiltration, recapitulating patient tumors. Furthermore, these tumors displayed intrinsic resistance to immune checkpoint blockade, potentially due to poor myeloid cell antigen presentation and T cell priming. Additionally, mEGFRvIII-PC cells were the most resistant to antigen-specific T cell-induced cytotoxicity and simultaneously promoted T cell exhaustion, while murine interferon-γ (mIFN-γ) stimulation induced a greater response in vitro with enhanced upregulation of PD-L1 relative to MHC-I. In sum, these findings demonstrate the improved fidelity of the mEGFRvIII-PC model to patient tumors and support its use in developing and refining novel therapeutic paradigms for GBM.

title: CDH1 loss remodels gene expression and lineage identity in human mammary epithelial cells [RNA-seq_siCDH1]
summary: Invasive lobular carcinoma (ILC) is a common subtype of breast cancer, molecularly defined by genetic loss of CDH1, and subsequent loss of cell adhesion protein E-cadherin, in ~95% of ILC. Consistent with the shift to a luminal progenitor phenotype, CDH1 loss enhanced proliferative capacity over the finite lifespan of the HMECs, highlighting a feature of early CDH1 loss that may contribute to clonal advantage during tumor initiation. Moreover, CDH1 loss enhanced anoikis resistance, a defining feature of ILC cells. title: Arginine Rewires eIF4F Translation Initiation to Overcome Fever-Induced CAR T-Cell Dysfunction
summary: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy has revolutionized treatment of hematological malignancies, but cytokine release syndrome (CRS) remains a major toxicity. Fever—a hallmark of CRS—has been understudied as a modifier of therapeutic efficacy. In a retrospective cohort of patients with B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia treated with CD22-directed CAR T-cells (NCT02315612), sustained high-grade fever inversely correlated with clinical response. Mechanistically, experimental hyperthermia impaired proximal CAR signaling, reduced cytotoxicity, and compromised metabolic fitness through dysregulated arginine metabolism. Arginine supplementation restored CAR T-cell function following hyperthermic stress and enhanced cytotoxicity under normothermic conditions. This effect required mTOR-dependent recruitment of the eIF4F translation initiation complex and downstream cMYC-driven metabolic reprogramming. Importantly, arginine enhanced GMP-manufactured CAR T-cell function under normothermia, while oral supplementation improved in vivo efficacy. These findings identify metabolic control of translation as a fever-sensitive checkpoint and establish arginine supplementation as a tractable strategy to enhance CAR T-cell efficacy.

title: Paired Transcriptomic Profiling Identifies Shared Liver Metas-tasis-Associated Molecular Features in Colorectal Cancer
summary: Colorectal cancer liver metastasis (CCLM) is closely associated with poor patient prognosis, yet patient-specific molecular heterogeneity complicates the identification of recurrent molecular changes during metastasis. title: p38α Signaling Is Associated with Pancreatic Ductal Adeno-carcinoma Progression and Represents a Potential Therapeutic Vulnerability
summary: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is one of the most lethal malignancies, and approximately 15% of cases arise from intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasms (IP-MNs). These precursor lesions can progress to invasive cancer through the accumulation of molecular alterations. Immunohistochemical analyses confirmed increased phospho-activated p38α in PDAC tissues, particularly in lesions with advanced malig-nant features, while PDAC cell lines displayed higher levels of activated p38α than non-tumorigenic pancreatic epithelial cells. Pharmacological inhibition of p38α sup-pressed downstream MAPKAPK2 phosphorylation, induced apoptotic cell death, and re-duced tumorsphere growth and viability. Consistently, PDTOs exhibiting elevated p38α activation showed increased sensitivity to ralimetinib treatment. Collectively, these find-ings identify p38α signaling as a pathway activated during PDAC progression and sup-port further investigation of p38α-targeted therapies as a potential precision medicine strategy for pancreatic cancer.

title: Genetic variants within silencer elements contribute to human blood cell traits
summary: Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have identified numerous non-coding loci associated with human complex traits and diseases. However, assigning regulatory functions to causal variants remains challenging, historical efforts have largely focused on promoters and enhancers, often overlooking the regulatory impact of silencers. In this study, we performed high-throughput screening to characterize changes in potential silencer activities within 14,720 fine-mapped causal non-coding single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) associated with 15 diverse blood traits. We have prioritized 805 blood trait-associated non-coding SNPs link to changes in putative silencer activity (425 loss-of-function and 380 gain-of-function). Using targeted mutagenesis in orthogonal episomal reporter assays and endogenous knock-in via CRISPR-Cas9 editing, we validated the allelic imbalances in silencer activity of identified silencer-disruptive variants. We demonstrated that a silencer-disruptive variant rs2857078 can impair red blood cell maturation and hemoglobin synthesis using an in vitro K562 erythroid differentiation model. To prioritize pathogenic variants within silencer elements, we trained a machine learning model using evolutionary conservation metrics and single-cell chromatin accessibility profiles across the hematopoietic hierarchy. Taken together, our study underscores the importance of investigating functions of silencer variants in post-GWAS functional studies.

summary: Most solid tumors resist immunotherapy. Immune engagers redirect lymphocytes against cancer, but poor tumor access, immunosuppression and systemic toxicity constrain efficacy. title: Pannexin 1 Ablation Disrupts Cell Cycle Progression and Compromises the Structure of Melanoma Tumours
summary: Pannexin 1 (PANX1) is a channel-forming glycoprotein that has been implicated in regulating melanoma cell properties such as growth, migration, and invasion. Our findings indicate that PANX1 regulates cell cycle progression and the structural architecture of A375-P melanoma tumours, highlighting the therapeutic utility of targeting PANX1 in melanoma.

title: Age-dependent differences in SARS-CoV-2 entry-factor expression and innate immune responses between pediatric and adult liver organoids
summary: Background Since early 2022, a global surge in cases of severe acute hepatitis of unknown origin (AHUO) in children has been reported, with no definitive aetiology established. Epidemiological evidence suggests a potential link to SARS CoV 2 infection, particularly during Omicron-predominant periods, yet the mechanisms underlying the apparently higher susceptibility of children to SARS CoV 2 related liver injury remain poorly understood. This study used normal liver organoids derived from paediatric and adult donors to compare the infectivity and host immune responses to SARS CoV 2 wild type (WT) and Omicron (BA.1/BA.2) variants, aiming to explore the possible role of SARS CoV 2 in paediatric acute hepatitis. Methods Liver organoids were established from adjacent normal tissues of three adult patients with hepatocellular carcinoma and three paediatric patients with hepatoblastoma, collected between February and December 2022. Organoids were infected with SARS-CoV 2 WT, Omicron BA.1 or BA.2 at a multiplicity of infection (MOI) of 0.1. Viral loads in supernatants and intracellular viral RNA were quantified by RT qPCR at 24 and 48 hours post infection (hpi). At 48 hpi, RNA seq was performed to profile transcriptomic changes and pathway enrichment. Additionally, single cell RNA seq data were used to compare baseline expression of SARS CoV 2 entry associated genes between paediatric and adult hepatocytes. Results Paediatric hepatocytes showed significantly higher basal expression of entry related genes, including ASGR1, KREMEN1, CTSB, CTSL, and VIM, than adult cells. Both paediatric and adult liver organoids were permissive to WT and Omicron, but Omicron BA.1/BA.2 yielded higher intracellular viral RNA levels than WT, with notably higher intracellular viral RNA burden in paediatric organoids. RNA seq revealed that Omicron infection induced a more robust innate immune and inflammatory response in paediatric organoids—encompassing interferon signalling, RIG I like receptor and Toll like receptor pathways—alongside relative downregulation of adaptive immune-pathway transcripts. In adult organoids, transcriptomic divergence between Omicron and WT was less pronounced. Compared with adults, Omicron infected paediatric organoids upregulated interferon γ signalling and innate immune system components, while downregulating adaptive immune-pathway transcripts; key receptors such as ACE2 and TMPRSS4 remained consistently higher in paediatric organoids across all viral strains.

title: Identification of heterogeneous subtypes of human dendritic cells from the lymph nodes of patients with gastric cancer
summary: The subtypes of heterogeneous conventional dendritic cells (cDCs) and plasmacytoid dendritic cells (pDCs) in lymph nodes (LNs) are difficult to distinguish because they share similar surface markers. This study aimed to identify cDCs, pDCs, and other cell types in dendritic cell (DC)-enriched LNs from patients with gastric cancer (GC) by analyzing surface markers and gene expression. Expression of surface markers, including CD141, CD1c, and CD123, in DC-enriched cells was analyzed by conventional flow cytometry and by BD AbSeq using antibody-derived tags, and simultaneous single-cell transcriptome and epitope profiling was used to characterize DC subtypes. DC-enriched cells showed CD1c+CD141+ and CD141+CD123+ populations. A clustering approach based on antibody-derived tags identified 17 clusters with single- and double-positive DC surface markers, and combined transcriptome and epitope analyses identified 26 clusters with distinct surface marker and gene expression profiles. DC lineages included subtypes distinct from the typical cDC1, cDC2, and pDC types. A proportion of CD1c-expressing cDC2 lineage cells expressed surface features characteristic of cDC1 and pDC, and CD1c expression was observed in cell types other than DC lineages. Differences in DC cluster frequencies were not significant across clinical stages and molecular subtypes of gastric cancer. The mRNA expression pattern of the CD141+ cDC1 lineage distinguished it from the CD1c+ cDC2 lineage and resolved clusters with transitional states within both lineages. Transcripts related to DC maturation and migration were detected in a CD137+ DC subtype that highly expressed HLA-DR and CD137. Cluster analysis of DC-enriched cells in LNs revealed subtypes of the cDC1, cDC2, and pDC lineages, distinctive DC subtypes in a transitional state between cDC1 and cDC2, and a CD137+ DC subset with mature and migratory features.

title: PCNA Inhibition Enhances the Antitumor Activity of KRAS-Targeted Therapies in Pancreatic Cancer
summary: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is an aggressive disease with a dismal prognosis. More than 90% of PDAC tumors harbor KRAS mutations, and several KRAS inhibitors (KRASi), including mutation-specific (sotorasib, MRTX1133, RMC-9805), and pan-RAS (RMC-6236) inhibitors, are being tested clinically and preclinically. However, response to single-agent KRASi is suboptimal, underscoring the need for novel combination therapies to improve treatment outcomes. Proliferating cell nuclear antigen (PCNA) is a ring-shaped clamp protein that regulates DNA replication, repair, and resolution of transcription-replication conflict, which are critical processes for pancreatic cancer survival. AOH1996 is a first-in-class, selective PCNA inhibitor in phase I clinical trials. Here, we found that treatment with AOH1996 is efficacious in various PDAC models in vitro. PCNA and KRAS are predicted to be synthetic lethal partners, and RNA sequencing reveals the enrichment of MAPK and PI3K signaling pathways in AOH1996-treated cells. Combination of AOH1996 with KRASi demonstrates strong synergy across KRAS G12C and G12D models. Treatment with a combination of AOH1996 and KRASi induces cell cycle arrest and apoptosis in PDAC cells. In vivo, combining subtherapeutic doses of AOH1996 with sotorasib, MRTX1133, RMC-9805 (zoldonrasib) or RMC-6236 (daraxonrasib) reduced tumor growth rates without any significant toxicity. Residual tumor analysis showed sustained pERK and Myc inhibition in the combination arm. In conclusion, combination of AOH1996 with KRAS inhibitors is a promising therapeutic strategy for KRAS-driven PDAC that could improve responses and patient outcomes, thus warranting further clinical investigation.

title: Comparative Analysis of Primary and Liver Fibroblasts Reveals MET as a Potent Target in Pancreatic Cancer Metastasis [RNA-Seq]
summary: The tumor microenvironment drives many malignant features of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC). The fibroblasts within pancreatic tumors promote tissue remodeling, immune suppression, and resistance to therapy. However, the interactions between stromal populations and pancreatic cancer cells are less understood in the liver, the most frequent site of PDAC metastasis. To address this, we employ single cell transcriptomics to compare primary pancreatic vs. liver PDAC lesions. Using a ligand-receptor interaction tool, we assess upregulated pathways in liver PDAC. Here, we identify the expression of hepatocyte growth factor (HGF) in fibroblasts and its receptor MET in cancer cells are both markedly increased in the PDAC liver niche. Using functional assays, we validate that mitogenic MET signaling is activated in PDAC cells by liver-derived fibroblasts. Importantly, the inhibition of MET signaling leads to reduced tumor growth in immune competent mouse models. Collectively, our data demonstrates that liver stromal-epithelial crosstalk networks engage in signaling pathways distinct from primary pancreatic tumors, highlighting opportunities to develop new treatments for metastatic disease.

title: Cancer-Associated Transcriptional Readthrough Reveals Distinct Stress- and Proliferation-Related Programs
summary: Transcriptional readthrough generates downstream-of-gene (DoG) RNAs through transcription beyond canonical termination sites. Although DoGs have been implicated in cellular stress and cancer, their biological and clinical significance remains poorly understood. We analyzed DoG transcripts in 787 experimental and 3,066 public RNA-seq profiles encompassing colorectal, lung, pancreatic, stomach, and thyroid cancers. RNA-seq library design strongly influenced DoG detection, with rRNA-depleted and paired-end libraries providing greater sensitivity than poly(A)-selected and single-end approaches. DoG abundance and expression were increased in most cancer types, whereas DoG length was largely unchanged. Joint analysis of DoG and parental gene expression identified two distinct classes of cancer-associated readthrough. DoGs upregulated independently of parental genes, consistent with dysregulated transcription termination, included 31 transcripts recurrently increased across all five cancer types and were associated with stress-related functions. In contrast, DoGs co-upregulated with their parental genes were enriched for proliferation-related processes. In an experimental cohort of 95 lung cancer patients receiving PD-(L)1 immune checkpoint therapy, higher abundance and expression of recurrent DoG signatures were associated with shorter progression-free survival (HR 2.53–3.24). These findings reveal distinct biological components of cancer-associated transcriptional readthrough and identify recurrent DoG signatures as candidate prognostic biomarkers.

title: Covalent targeting of the SKP1-βTrCP interface activates NRF1/2 signaling [IMR32]
summary: The cap’n’collar family of bZIP transcription factors, including NRF1 and NRF2, execute essential protective transcriptional programs in response to cellular stressors and are thus of high interest to harness with pharmacological tools. title: Shared molecular regulation of quiescence in neural and glioma stem cells reveals therapeutic vulnerabilities
summary: Quiescent glioma cells evade chemoradiation and drive glioblastoma recurrence by reactivating to repopulate the tumour, but are hard to study due to their rarity and difficulty maintaining quiescence in vitro. We hypothesised that quiescence programs conserved between neural stem cells and glioma cells could be exploited to lock glioma cells in quiescence and prevent reactivation. Using single-cell RNA-sequencing and patient-derived glioma stem cell lines, we found that although glioma cells resist entering deep quiescence, they share conserved activation trajectories with neural stem cells. Because this conservation lets a tractable neural progenitor line act as a surrogate for rare quiescent glioma cells, we queried LINCS L1000 signatures across more than 3,000 compounds and validated the top classes (mTOR, ATPase and histone lysine methyltransferase inhibitors) as quiescence promoters in glioma stem cell lines. By establishing conserved activation programs and enabling cross-cell-type screening, our work provides a strategy for driving therapy-resistant glioma cells into quiescence.

title: SCOPE-Based Target and Pathway Enrichment Identifies the Histamine H1 Receptor as a Regulator of Exodosis
summary: Phenotypic screening enables discovery of small molecules without requiring predefined targets, but mechanistic interpretation remains challenging due to polypharmacology and pathway complexity. We developed SCOPE (Screening Compound Ontology for Pathway Enrichment), a KNIME-based computational framework that links compound-level screening data to annotated targets and pathways to facilitate generation of mechanistic hypotheses. SCOPE integrates multi-source target annotations and performs sequential target- and pathway-level statistical enrichment using the screened compound library as the background to prioritize shared mechanisms of action. Applied to a previously established high-throughput screen for modulators of endoplasmic reticulum (ER)-stress induced secretion of ER resident proteins, a process known as exodosis, SCOPE identified calcium signaling as the most enriched KEGG pathway without prior biological context. Its target enrichment revealed several G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) linked to inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate receptors (IP3Rs)- mediated calcium signaling, with widespread antagonism of these receptors among compounds that reduced exodosis, implicating this pathway in the regulation of exodosis. Notably, SCOPE uncovered a novel role for the histamine receptor HRH1 in exodosis, which was validated by RNAi knockdown, gene knockout, and pharmacological modulation, implicating HRH1 as a potential therapeutic target for modulating exodosis. These results highlight SCOPE’s potential to prioritize experimentally testable targets and pathways from phenotypic screening data.

title: GITRL-armored anti-GD2 CAR-NK cells exhibit adaptive transcriptional remodeling and enhanced activity in 3D solid tumor models
summary: The immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment remains a major obstacle to the efficacy of chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-based therapies against solid tumors. We developed a fourth-generation anti-GD2 CAR co-expressing GITRL, evaluated in NK-92 cells and primary NK cells. CAR expression increased cytotoxicity; although CAR.GD2 showed the strongest immediate cytotoxicity in two-dimensional assays, CAR.GD2.GITRL demonstrated superior tumor control in a three-dimensional model. In vivo, both CAR-NK-92 groups significantly delayed tumor growth versus parental cells, without differing from each other. To investigate the immunomodulatory activity of GITRL, induced regulatory T cells (iTreg) were generated. GITRL reduced Treg-mediated suppression of CAR-T cell proliferation, confirming the functionality of GITR/GITRL interaction, however in NK cells, CAR expression itself was sufficient to confer this resistance, preventing the identification of an additional GITRL-specific effect. These results support GITRL-armored anti-GD2 CAR-NK cells as a promising allogeneic immunotherapy platform for solid tumors and support a rationale for further evaluation in more physiologically relevant tumor models.

title: Massively parallel characterization epistatic effects of close proximity variant pairs on gene expression
summary: Precise control of gene expression relies in part on cis-regulatory elements (CREs), including enhancers. Genetic variation within enhancers can alter their regulatory activity and contribute to variation in gene expression, yet the effects of multiple nearby variants within the same enhancer remain poorly understood. Most studies using functional assays, including massively parallel reporter assays (MPRAs), have examined the effects of individual variants, leaving the combined effects of nearby variants largely unexplored. Here, we addressed this by measuring the regulatory activity of all four haplotypes for 7,285 pairs of closely spaced single-nucleotide variants (SNVs) identified from whole-genome sequencing data of 2,420 Estonian Biobank participants. In K562 cells, regulatory effects were widespread, with 57% of tested variant pairs having at least one haplotype that differed significantly in activity from the ancestral haplotype. The effects of individual variants frequently depended on the allelic background provided by the neighboring variant, with some variants showing opposite effects in different allelic backgrounds. Among a smaller high-confidence subset selected for analysis of additivity, 59% (105/178) of variant pairs showed non-additive effects, which were associated in part with the distance between the variants. These interactions were predominantly sub-additive, with double-derived haplotypes typically showing smaller effects than expected from the individual variant effects. Together, our results demonstrate that nearby variants within the same enhancer can jointly shape regulatory activity and highlight the importance of considering local allelic context when interpreting the functional effects of regulatory variation.

title: Tumor-derived UCHL1 promotes tolerogenic DC maturation and crosstalk with Tregs to suppress anti-tumor immunity
summary: Although immune-checkpoint blockade therapies have revolutionized cancer treatment, many patients fail to respond, highlighting the need to identify predictive biomarkers and target mechanisms that limit treatment efficacy. Here, we investigated the mechanisms underlying resistance to atezolizumab plus bevacizumab (Atezo/Bev) therapy in advanced hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). We profiled tumor ecosystems using single-cell RNA sequencing and mass cytometry by time-of-flight from a cohort of patients with advanced HCC receiving Atezo/Bev, integrating these data with external single-cell datasets. Tumor cells upregulated ubiquitin C-terminal hydrolase L1 (UCHL1), which subverted immune surveillance by driving conventional dendritic cell transformation into mature dendritic cells enriched in immunoregulatory molecules (mregDCs) and promoting mregDC and regulatory T (Treg) cell crosstalk, thereby restraining CD8+ T cell anti-tumor immunity. Mechanistically, UCHL1 enhanced glycolysis and lactate accumulation by stabilizing hypoxia-inducible factor 1-alpha, which promoted sterol regulatory element-binding protein 2 activation and nuclear translocation in dendritic cells, inducing tolerogenic maturation. Genetic ablation or pharmacological inhibition of UCHL1 reduced mregDC and Treg accumulation, safeguarding anti-tumor immunity and sensitizing mouse models to Atezo/Bev therapy. Furthermore, pre-treatment plasma UCHL1 levels predicted clinical response to Atezo/Bev therapy in a phase III HCC trial. UCHL1 drives immunotherapy resistance through mregDC-mediated immune suppression, making it a viable therapeutic target and predictive biomarker for Atezo/Bev treatment in HCC.

title: Clinical-scale manufacturing of CD137+ enriched tumor-reactive T cells for glioblastoma in the CliniMACS Prodigy System
summary: The majority of tumor infiltrating lymphocyte (TIL) studies and therapies are conducted in tumors with high T cell infiltration and a large mutational burdens. This study demonstrates how a novel manufacturing process which enriches anti-tumor reactivity can allow robust, clinical-scale production of a potent TIL products for glioblastoma (GBM), a immunologically cold, poorly infiltrated and low-mutational burden tumor. Ultrasonic surgical aspirates (UA), routinely collected during GBM resections, were identified as a reliable source of TILs for clinical manufacturing. TILs were generated from GBM UA in GMP-like conditions and at clinical scale and using the closed and automated TRT Process on the CliniMACS Prodigy. Further, matched TIL products were generated, at full GMP scale, which were enriched for CD137+ cells, depleted for CD137+ or not-enriched. These products were then extensively characterized and tested in downstream functional assay for potency against autologous and non-autologous patient-derived cell lines. Cellular and transcriptomic analyses revealed that UA-derived CD137 (4-1BB/TNFRSF9)+ T cells are clonally expanded, exhibit activation and memory phenotypes, and express transcriptional profiles associated with tumor reactivity. Importantly, the fully closed and GMP compliant process maintained favorable therapeutic markers previously correlated with clinical benefit in other TIL indications. Functional assays confirmed potent and specific cytotoxicity of CD137+ TRTs against autologous GBM cell lines, relative to TILs generated without selection.
