title: Transitions between cancer stem cells and non-cancer stem cells during metastasis
summary: Cancer stem cells (CSCs) and non-cancer stem cells (nCSCs) exhibit dynamic bidirectional transitions during metastasis, yet the mechanisms and therapeutic implications of this interconversion remain poorly understood. title: INTS12 is the stabilisation factor for Integrator at promoter-proximal sites [A_3prime_rnaseq_arrayed_crisprscreen_integrator_subunits]
summary: Promoter-proximal RNA Polymerase II (RNAPII) pausing and processivity are controlled by distinct modules of the Integrator complex, which together fine-tune transcription and protect against the accumulation of defective RNAPII complexes. Compromised activity of individual Integrator modules has been linked to human disease including cancer and developmental disorders, caused by defective transcription of protein-coding and small-nuclear RNAs. Despite extensive genetic and structural characterisation of Integrator, how it is recruited to promoter-proximal sites and subsequently evicted remains poorly understood. Here, we identify INTS12, together with INTS1, as the stabilisation module for Integrator at promoter-proximal sites. INTS12 bridges Integrator to paused elongation complex through its N-terminus, which binds INTS1, and its PHD domain which binds NELFA directly, thereby safeguarding against the release of defective RNAPII complexes into elongation. Acute degradation of INTS12 selectively dissociates Integrator from the pre-termination complexes, which remain sensitive to CDK9-mediated pause release, indicating an interconversion between paused RNAPII states. In the absence of INTS12, excessive CDK9-mediated pause release is toxic to cells, and its suppression offsets Integrator deficiency. Together, these findings delineate a catch and release mechanism for Integrator and reveal a dynamic interconversion between canonical paused RNAPII and paused-Integrator states. The interplay between these processes and P-TEFb-mediated pause-release ensures that only transcription-competent complexes are released into elongation.

summary: Durable remission after CD19-directed CAR T (CAR19) therapy is linked to long-term persistence, yet the cellular states and drivers of persistence remain poorly defined. title: A Rhein–Cisplatin Pt(IV) Conjugate Reprograms Platinum–DNA Interactions to Amplify DNA Damage in Pancreatic Cancer
summary: Pancreatic cancer exhibits profound resistance to platinum-based chemotherapy owing to efficient DNA damage repair and replication stress tolerance. Here, we report a strategy that reprograms platinum–DNA interactions by incorporating a DNA-interacting natural product ligand into a Pt(IV) scaffold. CPR exhibited potent antitumor activity in pancreatic cancer cells and tumor-bearing mice, including strong cytotoxicity against the relatively cisplatin-refractory PANC-1 cell line. By integrating molecular simulations, DNA minor-groove binding assays, reduction studies, cellular platinum uptake analysis and nuclear enrichment of rhein, we established a molecular-to-cellular evidence chain showing that CPR enables coordinated DNA engagement by both rhein and platinum. This dual DNA-level interaction amplified DNA structural perturbation and replication-associated damage, leading to DDR activation, repair overload, G2/M arrest, apoptosis, and tumor suppression. RNA-seq analysis, biochemical assays immunoblot analysis, and immunofluorescence imaging collectively revealed robust γ-H2AX accumulation, RAD51 recruitment, and activation of DNA repair pathways. However, the sustained DNA damage and replication stress induced by CPR exceeded the repair capacity of pancreatic cancer cells, resulting in DNA damage–repair imbalance. title: Performance of the 10X Genomics Flex Single-Cell Sequencing Assay and its Application to Overcome Challenges in Clinical Trial Samples
summary: Background: Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) has become essential for understanding disease biology, yet its application in clinical trials is often limited by logistical challenges associated with the handling of biospecimens. Newly developed protocols aim to address these limitations by enabling profiling of fixed tissue. These new solutions need to be benchmarked against well-established protocols to assess their performance and suitability for clinical research. Results: In the present study we systematically compared different fixed-tissue and nuclei-based RNA-sequencing workflows in a set of solid tumor samples, which were collected and preserved following common procedures in clinical trials. When applied to both frozen tumor tissue and FFPE blocks, the 10X Genomics GEM-X Flex Gene Expression assay, in combination with the "chop-fix" preprocessing protocol, demonstrated enhanced data quality - characterized by higher gene and UMI detection sensitivity and slightly reduced ambient RNA background - relative to the standard GEM-X Universal Gene Expression solution. Furthermore, this protocol improved the capture of specific biological signals and resolved cell states that were less distinct with conventional approaches. Conclusions: GEM-X Flex generates reliable, comprehensive transcriptomic data from both fixed tissue and clinical biopsies. By overcoming some of the limitations of fresh and frozen tissue analysis, this protocol offers a robust solution for the broad implementation of scRNA-seq in clinical trials. Data in this series: only the first benchmark experiment of the study, i.e. 4 libraries from one lung tumor sample (Patient1); the FFPE and other samples of the study are not included.

title: Paralog-targeting in vivo CRISPR screens identify RNF19A/RNF19B as functionally redundant suppressors of anti-tumor immunity
summary: Functional redundancy among paralogous genes poses a major obstacle to identifying regulators of tumor immunity, as loss of a single gene is often insufficient to elicit a phenotype. We systematically interrogated paralog redundancy in cancer immune evasion using large-scale paralog-targeting in vivo CRISPR screens. Employing multiplexed CRISPR editing with Cas9 and Cas12a, we evaluated single- and paired-gene knockouts across 2,147 paralog pairs in multiple syngeneic tumor models treated with immune checkpoint blockade (ICB). This approach uncovered known and novel paralog pairs whose simultaneous loss, but not individual deletion, markedly enhanced anti-tumor immunity. We identified the E3 ubiquitin ligases RNF19A and RNF19B as previously unrecognized, functionally redundant tumor-intrinsic suppressors of ICB efficacy. Dual loss of RNF19A and RNF19B sensitized diverse tumor models to immunotherapy. Mechanistically, RNF19A and RNF19B limit the surface abundance of immune receptors, including IFNGR1/IFNGR2, TNFR1, and Lymphotoxin Beta Receptor (LTβR), by promoting their lysosomal degradation. Increased expression of these receptors on RNF19A/RNF19B-deficient tumor cells resulted in heightened sensitivity to inflammatory cytokines and T cell-mediated killing. Surprisingly, we found that loss of RNF19A/RNF19B in immune cells further augmented immunotherapy response by dramatically increasing the cell surface expression of 4-1BB and IFNGR1, and enhancing effector function in T cells. Together, these findings establish paralog co-deletion as a powerful approach to uncover immune regulatory pathways masked by genetic redundancy. Our study identifies RNF19A and RNF19B as novel negative regulators of tumor-intrinsic and immune-specific effects and highlights paralog targeting as a promising strategy to enhance cancer immunotherapy.

title: Targeting the 9p24.1 Axis with JAK Inhibition and Immune Checkpoint Blockade in Lymphomas
summary: Amplification of chromosome 9p24.1 drives coordinated upregulation of JAK–STAT signaling and the immune checkpoint ligands PD-L1 and PD-L2, promoting lymphoma cell survival and immune evasion. While PD-1 blockade demonstrates substantial activity in 9p24.1-spectrum lymphomas, responses remain incomplete, particularly outside classical Hodgkin lymphoma. We hypothesized that dual targeting of the 9p24.1 axis through JAK1/2 inhibition could enhance immune checkpoint blockade by simultaneously disrupting tumor-intrinsic survival signaling and reprogramming the tumor microenvironment. Using 9p24.1-amplified lymphoma cell lines, bulk RNA sequencing, a three-dimensional immune co-culture organoid platform, ex vivo patient peripheral blood mononuclear cells, and complementary syngeneic and humanized murine models, the effects of ruxolitinib alone and in combination with pembrolizumab were evaluated. Ruxolitinib preferentially reduced PD-L1/PD-L2 and c-MYC expression in 9p24.1-amplified cell lines and induced transcriptional upregulation of antigen presentation pathways, including MHC class II–associated genes. In organoid co-culture systems, combination therapy enhanced CD3⁺ T cell tumor infiltration and increased tumor cell apoptosis compared with monotherapy. Within the peripheral immune milieu, ruxolitinib-containing regimens reduced regulatory T cells and myeloid-derived suppressor cells while increasing markers of both CD4+ and CD8+ T cell activation. In vivo, combination therapy suppressed tumor growth, prolonged survival, and was accompanied by increased intratumoral T cell activation, findings corroborated in spatial CosMx protein tissue microarray analysis. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that JAK inhibition remodels both tumor-intrinsic and immune microenvironment programs to enhance PD-1 blockade in 9p24.1 amplified lymphomas.

title: Targeting BMI1 enhances cell adhesion to inhibit colorectal cancer progression and improve the efficacy of cetuximab
summary: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is a common malignant tumor with poor prognosis, urgently requiring new biomarkers and therapeutic targets. This study investigated the role of BMI1 in the progression of colorectal cancer and its regulatory mechanisms, as well as evaluated whether targeting BMI1 can enhance the efficacy of first-line drugs. The combination of resveratrol and cetuximab exhibits synergistic antitumor effects both in cultured cells and in vivo. In summary, this study elucidates the intervention role of miR-218-5p as an upstream regulator of BMI1 and confirms that resveratrol’s targeted inhibition of BMI1 can enhance the therapeutic effect of cetuximab, providing new experimental evidence and strategies for molecular targeted combination therapy in colorectal cancer.

title: Study of LETT@MVs‑induced ferroptosis in tumor cells via supplementation of PUFA
summary: Ferroptosis represents a promising therapeutic strategy for cancer, yet its anti‑tumor efficacy is largely limited by insufficient polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFA) within the tumor microenvironment (TME). Aloe vera thylakoid membranes, naturally rich in PUFA, are an ideal source to facilitate robust lipid peroxidation. To address biological delivery obstacles, we constructed tumor‑targeting biomimetic microvesicles (LETT@MVs) by engineering aloe‑thylakoid‑derived microvesicles (TDMVs) with the multifunctional peptide LETT, which enables tumor‑targeted delivery and lysosomal escape. We systematically characterized the influences of LETT@MVs on hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) cells, including cell viability, vasculogenic mimicry (VM) formation, lipid peroxidation and ferroptosis in vitro. Antitumor potency and biosafety were further validated using an orthotopic HCC mouse model. Mechanistically, multi‑omics strategies combining bulk RNA‑seq, metabolomics and scRNA‑seq were applied to decipher underlying molecular events. LETT@MVs were effectively internalized by HCC cells and successfully escaped lysosomal degradation. Taking advantage of endogenous PUFA stored in thylakoid components, LETT@MVs triggered potent lipid peroxidation and ferroptosis, meanwhile remodelled the extracellular matrix (ECM) to suppress vasculogenic mimicry. In orthotopic HCC mice, LETT@MVs markedly retarded tumor growth via ferroptosis induction and VM repression without obvious safety risks. Integrated multi‑omics data demonstrated that LETT@MVs rewired transcriptional and metabolic profiles of HCC cells, driving highly‑metabolic tumor cells toward ferroptotic stress status and generating near‑death cell subpopulations. Collectively, our work validates that aloe‑thylakoid‑originated biomimetic nanoplatform can trigger robust tumor ferroptosis through PUFA supplementation, providing new clues to conquer ferroptosis resistance and advance therapeutic interventions for hyper‑metabolic tumors.

title: Metabolic rewiring that protects against ferroptosis underlies resistance to CDK4/6 inhibition in prostate cancer
summary: The G1/S phase transition of the cell cycle, controlled by cyclin-dependent kinase 4/6 (CDK4/6), is frequently deregulated in metastatic prostate cancers, establishing a rationale for CDK4/6 inhibition as a therapeutic strategy. title: H3K27me3 Drives Constricted Migration–Induced 3D Genome Rewiring in Melanoma [RNA-Seq]
summary: Repeated exposure of neoplastic cells to mechanical stresses during metastasis can drive stable morphological and physiological changes. We previously showed that A375 human melanoma cells subjected to 10 rounds of constricted migration (“Bottom-10 cells”) became significantly more migratory and exhibited H3K9me3 relocalization, transcriptional remodeling, and chromatin compartment changes relative to naïve parental A375 cells. Because these phenotypes persist across cell divisions, we hypothesized they are driven and maintained by specific epigenetic mechanisms. Here, we profiled candidate histone modifications by CUT&RUN and applied a computational model to identify marks that explain compartment switches. In parental cells, H3K9me3 and H3K4me1 strongly predict locus stability in the B and A compartments, respectively. In contrast, changes in H3K27me3 dynamically predict A-to-B compartment switching after constricted migration. Consistently, altered H3K27me3 enrichment correlates with both differentially regulated genes and chromatin compartment changes between Bottom-10 and parental populations. We therefore tested whether inhibiting H3K27me3 deposition alters migratory potential and/or the “memory” of the increased migratory phenotype. Inhibiting EZH1/2 reduced migration efficiency overall, with a stronger effect on constricted than unconstricted migration. This reduction was accompanied by decreased genomic H3K27me3 enrichment and reversal of some compartment changes in Bottom-10 cells. However, acute treatment did not durably reverse the highly migratory Bottom-10 phenotype; cells returned to their initial state after drug removal. Chronic inhibition across many sequential rounds of constricted migration dramatically reduced the fraction of cells able to migrate. Notably, cells that migrated despite chronic EZH inhibition appeared to escape treatment, acquiring many typical Bottom-10 H3K27me3 and compartment changes even though acute inhibition tends to prevent them. Overall, these results highlight H3K27me3 as a key contributor to establishing and maintaining constricted migration–induced 3D genome changes.

title: Proteasomes in extracellular vesicles mediate most transcriptional effects in recipient colorectal cancer cells
summary: Extracellular vesicles (EVs) transmit lipids, proteins and RNA between cells of the organism. Among their cargo, EVs contain different forms of proteasomes - multi-subunit protein complexes responsible for degradation of most intracellular proteins. The transmission of proteasomes by EVs from one cell to another has been recently shown; however the biological significance of the phenomenon is generally unknown. Here we purified EVs from control colorectal adenocarcinoma cells and cells treated with IFN-γ, a cytokine known to activate expression of specific proteasome forms - non-constitutive proteasomes (ncPs). The obtained vesicles were incubated with two different irreversible proteasome inhibitors: carfilzomib and ONX-0914, targeting all forms and specifically ncPs, correspondingly. EVs were then incubated with control or carfilzomib-treated colorectal adenocarcinoma cells and the cellular RNA was obtained, followed by transcriptome acquisition and analysis. Incubation of control and carfilzomib-treated cells with treated or non-treated EVs obtained from control donor cells induced almost no effect on gene expression in recipient cells. However, vesicles obtained from IFN-γ-treated cells modulated expression of 53 genes in control cells and 2 genes in carfilzomib-treated cells. Treatment of vesicles with either one or another proteasome inhibitor affected the expression of 49 genes in control cells. In carfilzomib-treated cells inhibition of proteasomes in EVs affected 21 genes. Importantly, in both cases inhibition of ncPs in vesicles using ONX-0914 induced more pronounced effects on transcription in recipient cells. Most of the genes with differential expression were involved in oxidative phosphorylation. Obtained results indicate that most of the effects mediated in recipient cells by EVs were associated with the activity of proteasomes and specifically non-constitutive proteasomes, highlighting novel insights into EVs mediated proteasome transfer.

title: BAP1 safeguards double-strand DNA break repair by limiting DNA end resection
summary: The tumor suppressor BAP1 is frequently mutated in uveal melanoma and has been linked to homologous recombination (HR), yet how it influences DNA double-strand break (DSB) repair pathway choice remains unclear. Here, we identify BAP1 as a critical regulator that restricts DNA end resection to preserve non-homologous end-joining (NHEJ) capacity. Loss of BAP1 leads to aberrant accumulation of H2AK119 ubiquitination at DSBs, driving unscheduled resection in G1-phase cells and impairing recruitment of the anti-resection factor 53BP1. Co-depletion of the resection initiator CtIP restores NHEJ efficiency in BAP1-depleted cells, and pharmacological suppression of H2AK119 ubiquitination reverses these defects, placing unscheduled resection causally upstream of the end-joining failure. RNA sequencing and genome-wide H2AK119ub profiling show that neither the expression of NHEJ and HR genes nor the H2AK119ub landscape at their promoters is appreciably altered by BAP1 loss, supporting a role of altered H2AK119ub at the DSBs. These findings indicate that BAP1 safeguards DSB repair fidelity by preventing hyper-resection, thereby maintaining NHEJ competence. Consistent with this role, BAP1-depleted cells accumulate micronuclei, and BAP1 loss is associated with genomic instability in human uveal melanoma. Together, our results uncover a mechanism by which chromatin regulation constrains resection to coordinate repair pathway utilization.

title: Molecular analysis of gastric cancer identifies discrete subtypes associated with distinct clinical characteristics and survival outcomes: the ACRG (Asian Cancer Research Group) study [gastric tumors]
summary: Gastric cancer, a leading cause of cancer related deaths, is a heterogeneous disease, with little consensus on molecular subclasses and their clinical relevance. We describe four molecular subtypes linked with distinct patterns of molecular alterations, disease progression and prognosis viz. a) Microsatellite Instable: hypermutated intestinal subtype tumors occurring in antrum, best overall prognosis, lower frequency of recurrence (22%), with liver metastasis in 23% of recurred cases b) Mesenchymal-like: diffuse tumors with worst prognosis, a tendency to occur at an earlier age and highest recurrence (63%) with peritoneal seeding in 64% of recurred cases, low frequency of molecular alterations c) TP53-inactive with TP53 loss, presence of focal amplifications and chromosomal instability d) TP53-active marked by EBV infection and PIK3CA mutations. The key molecular mechanisms and associated survival patterns are validated in multiple independent cohorts, to provide a consistent and unified framework for further preclinical and clinical research.

title: KRAS mutation-associated gene expression, p53 and STK11 mutations, proliferation and immune surveillance in lung adenocarcinoma
summary: While mutations in the KRAS oncogene are amongst the most prevalent in human cancer, there are few successful treatments to target these tumors. It is also likely that heterogeneity in KRAS-mutant tumor biology significantly contributes to the response to therapy. We hypothesized that presence of commonly co-occurring mutations in STK11 and TP53 tumor suppressors may represent a significant source of heterogeneity in KRAS-mutant tumors. To address this, we utilized a large cohort of resected tumors from 442 lung adenocarcinoma patients with data including annotation of prevalent driver mutations (KRAS, EGFR) and tumor suppressor mutations (STK11 and TP53), microarray-based gene expression and clinical covariates including overall survival (OS). Specifically, we determined impact of STK11 and TP53 mutations on a new KRAS mutation-associated gene expression signature as well as previously defined signatures of tumor cell proliferation and immune surveillance responses. Interestingly, STK11, but not TP53 mutations, were associated with highly elevated expression of KRAS mutation-associated genes. Mutations in TP53 and STK11 also impacted tumor biology regardless of KRAS status, with TP53 strongly associated with enhanced proliferation and STK11 with suppression of immune surveillance. These findings illustrate the remarkably distinct ways through which tumor suppressor mutations may contribute to heterogeneity in KRAS-mutant tumor biology. In addition, these studies point to novel associations between gene mutations and immune surveillance that could impact the response to immunotherapy.
